Put $\sigma=n\cdot y$, $R=|rn-y|$, $N=(rn-y)/R$, $v=u+\sigma/c$, and $\delta=(r-\sigma-R)/c$, so $u+r/c-R/c=v+\delta$. Since $r-\sigma\ge r-a\ge r/2$, the identity $R^2=(r-\sigma)^2+|y|^2-\sigma^2$ gives $|R-(r-\sigma)|=(|y|^2-\sigma^2)/(R+r-\sigma)\le a^2/r$; hence $|\delta|\le a^2/(rc)\le a/(2c)$. Also $|r-R|\le|\sigma|+a^2/r\le3a/2$, so $R\ge r/2$, $|N-n|\le|(r-R)n-y|/R\le5a/r$, $|R^{-1}-r^{-1}|=|r-R|/(rR)\le3a/r^2$, and $|N/R-n/r|\le|N-n|/R+|R^{-1}-r^{-1}|\le13a/r^2$. Thus all retarded source arguments and the intervals between them lie in $K^\sharp$.

Retarded-field integrals. Put $C_a:=\overline B_a=\{y:|y|\le a\}$. If $|z|>a$, the ball of radius $(|z|-a)/2$ around $z$ is disjoint from $C_a$: the triangle inequality gives $|y|\ge|z|-|y-z|>a$ on that ball. Thus $C_a$ is closed. Also $C_a\subset B_{2a}$ since $a>0$, so it is bounded and hence compact by [F11]. A closed set is Borel, because its complement is open and the Borel sigma-algebra is closed under complements; under [A1], [F11] therefore makes $C_a$ Lebesgue measurable. The open ball $B_{2a}$ is measurable and has finite measure by [F7]. Applying measure monotonicity [F11] to $C_a\subset B_{2a}$ gives $\lambda_3(C_a)\le\lambda_3(B_{2a})<\infty$. These are exactly the compactness, measurability and finite-measure hypotheses needed for the set form of [F4]. Since $ho,J$ are jointly smooth and vanish for $|y|>a$, their values and their time derivatives vanish on $\partial B_a$; hence the potential integrals and the integrals obtained by one $x$- or $t$-derivative have the same values over $B_a$ and $\overline B_a$. Fix an observation event with $|x|>a$ and a product neighborhood with compact closure in the exterior region $|x|>a$. For each observation coordinate $x_i$ and $t$, hold the other coordinates fixed and apply the set form of [F4] on $\overline B_a$ with that coordinate as parameter. The retarded integrands and their parameter derivatives are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a$ times the chosen parameter interval, since $R=|x-y|>0$ there. Apply this argument to $ho$ and separately to each component of $J$, for each spatial-coordinate and time derivative needed in $
abla\varphi$, $\partial_tA$ and $\operatorname{curl}A$. The chain rule and algebra of derivatives give $
abla_xR=N$, $
abla_x(t-R/c)=-N/c$, and $
abla_x(R^{-1})=-N/R^2$. Substitution in $E=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ therefore gives, at $x=rn$, $t=u+r/c$, $\displaystyle E= rac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}\left( rac{c^2Nho_{\mathrm{ret}}}{R^2}+ rac{cNho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}}{R}- rac{J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}}{R}ight)dy,\qquad B=- rac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}N	imes\left( rac{J_{\mathrm{ret}}}{R^2}+ rac{J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}}{cR}ight)dy,$ where the subscript “ret” means evaluation at $v+\delta$. Here $R\ge r-a>0$ for $r\ge2a$.

Differentiation of the retarded current moment. Choose a bounded open interval $U$ containing $K$ and a compact interval $K_0$ whose interior contains $U$. Since $J$ and $J_t$ vanish on $\partial B_a$ by the smooth spatial-support hypothesis, the integral over $B_a$ agrees with that over the compact measurable finite-measure set $\overline B_a$ established in step 1.2. For fixed $n\in S^2$, the map $(y,u)\mapsto J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ and its $u$ derivative $J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ are continuous on a neighborhood of $\overline B_a\times K_0$. Apply the set form of [F4] separately to each of the three vector components with integration set $\overline B_a$ and parameter $u$. Thus $\partial_u I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ for every $u\in U$, so the definition of $V$ in the Statement is well-defined on a neighborhood of $K$.

Continuity identity for the shifted source. Fix $n,u$ and choose $R_0>a$. The $C^1$ vector field $y\mapsto J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ is zero near $\partial B_{R_0}$. Its divergence is $\operatorname{div}_yJ(y,v)+(n/c)\cdot J_t(y,v)=-\rho_t(y,v)+(n/c)\cdot J_t(y,v)$ by the chain rule and continuity. The divergence theorem gives zero for its integral over $B_{R_0}$, and the integrand is zero outside $B_a$; therefore $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,v)\,dy=(1/c)n\cdot\int_{B_a}J_t(y,v)\,dy=(1/c)n\cdot V(n,u)$.

Electric leading field and its remainder. Put $F_{\mathrm{lead}}:=r^{-1}(cn\rho_t(y,v)-J_t(y,v))$ inside the integrand of step 1.2. By step 1.4, its integral is $r^{-1}(n(n\cdot V)-V)=r^{-1}n\times(n\times V)$. For the first term of the exact integrand, $c^2|N\rho_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2|\le4c^2M_{\rho,0}/r^2$. For its second term, split $\displaystyle \frac{cN\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}}{R}-\frac{cn\rho_t(y,v)}r=c\left(\frac NR-\frac nr\right)\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}+\frac{cn}{r}\bigl(\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-\rho_t(y,v)\bigr);$ the first summand is bounded by $13caM_{\rho,1}/r^2$, while the scalar mean value theorem and step 1.1 bound the second by $a^2M_{\rho,2}/r^2$. For the third term, set $\Delta:=J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-J_t(y,v)$. If $\Delta\ne0$, put $e=\Delta/|\Delta|$ and apply the scalar mean value theorem to $s\mapsto e\cdot J_t(y,s)$ between $v$ and $v+\delta$; Cauchy–Schwarz then gives $|\Delta|=|e\cdot\Delta|\le M_{J,2}|\delta|$. The same bound is trivial for $\Delta=0$. Hence $\displaystyle \left|\frac{J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}}{R}-\frac{J_t(y,v)}r\right|\le\left|\frac1R-\frac1r\right|M_{J,1}+\frac1rM_{J,2}|\delta|\le\frac{3aM_{J,1}+a^2M_{J,2}/c}{r^2}.$ Integrating these bounds with [F7] and multiplying by $\mu_0/(4\pi)$ proves the stated $\Gamma_E/r^2$ estimate.

Magnetic leading field and its remainder. By $n\times(n\times V)=n(n\cdot V)-V$, one has $n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}/c=-\mu_0(4\pi cr)^{-1}n\times V$, which is the leading part of the magnetic integral in step 1.2. The $J_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2$ term has norm at most $4M_{J,0}/r^2$. For the $J_t$ term, split its coefficient as $N/(cR)-n/(cr)$ plus the time shift $n/(cr)$. The geometric coefficient is bounded by $13a/(cr^2)$. For the time shift, the vector mean value argument of step 2.1 gives $|J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-J_t(y,v)|\le M_{J,2}|\delta|$, so its contribution is at most $a^2M_{J,2}/(c^2r^2)$. The cross product with a unit vector does not increase norm by [F5], so [F7] gives the stated $\Gamma_B/r^2$ estimate.

Radiation-data limits. Multiplying the electric estimate of step 2.1 by $r$ gives a uniform error at most $\Gamma_E/r$ on $S^2\times K$, which tends to zero; thus the uniform limit in [F10] is $E_{\mathrm{rad}}=\mu_0 n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi)$. Multiplying the magnetic estimate of step 3.1 by $r$ likewise gives the uniform limit $B_{\mathrm{rad}}=n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}/c$. Since $n\cdot(n\times(n\times V))=0$, the leading electric field is transverse.

Retarded-time flux. The map $(n,u)\mapsto V(n,u)$ is continuous on $S^2\times K$: its integrand is continuous on the compact product $\overline B_a\times S^2\times K^\sharp$, hence uniformly continuous by [F9], and the integral difference is bounded by $\lambda_3(B_a)$ times the uniform integrand difference, using linearity and the integral triangle inequality [F7]. It is also bounded there by $\lambda_3(B_a)M_{J,1}$. The field estimates of steps 2.1 and 3.1 yield $E=E_{\mathrm{rad}}/r+e$ and $B=B_{\mathrm{rad}}/r+b$, where $|e|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$ and $|b|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$ uniformly on $S^2\times K$. Put $C_E:=\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)M_{J,1}/(4\pi)$ and $C_B:=C_E/c$; then $|E_{\mathrm{rad}}|\le C_E$ and $|B_{\mathrm{rad}}|\le C_B$. Bilinearity and the cross-product norm bound [F5] give $\displaystyle \left|r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)-\frac1{\mu_0}n\cdot(E_{\mathrm{rad}}\times B_{\mathrm{rad}})\right|\le\frac{C_E\Gamma_B+C_B\Gamma_E}{\mu_0r}+\frac{\Gamma_E\Gamma_B}{\mu_0r^2},$ which tends to zero uniformly for $r\ge2a$. Bilinearity of the cross product gives $\displaystyle r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac1{\mu_0}n\cdot(E_{\mathrm{rad}}\times B_{\mathrm{rad}})+R(n,u,r)=\frac{|E_{\mathrm{rad}}|^2}{\mu_0c}+R(n,u,r),$ uniformly, where $|R(n,u,r)|$ is bounded by the preceding display. Since $B_{\mathrm{rad}}=n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}/c$ and $n\cdot E_{\mathrm{rad}}=0$, the determinant formula for the cross product gives $\displaystyle n\cdot(E_{\mathrm{rad}}\times(n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}))=\det[E_{\mathrm{rad}},n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}},n]=\det[n,E_{\mathrm{rad}},n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}]=|n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}|^2=|E_{\mathrm{rad}}|^2,$ where the middle equality is a cyclic permutation and the last follows from [F5]. The sphere has finite area $4\pi$ by [F8], so integrating the explicit uniform remainder makes it tend to zero. Finally $|E_{\mathrm{rad}}|^2=\mu_0^2|n\times V|^2/(16\pi^2)$ by [F5], which gives the asserted flux limit at fixed retarded time.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory frame and SI conventions be those of the framework, and let $\rho,J$ be a jointly smooth conserved volume source supported in $\overline B_a(0)$ in space at every time, for some $a>0$. Let $E,B$ be the retarded fields generated by that source. Write $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$, $r=|x|$, and $t=u+r/c$. If maps $E_{\mathrm{rad}},B_{\mathrm{rad}}:S^2\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfy

$$rE(rn,u+r/c)\longrightarrow E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u),\qquad rB(rn,u+r/c)\longrightarrow B_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)$$

uniformly in $n\in S^2$ and $u$ in every compact interval as $r\to\infty$, then $E_{\mathrm{rad}}$ and $B_{\mathrm{rad}}$ are the electric and magnetic radiation data at fixed retarded time. The scaled fields carry units $\mathrm V$ and $\mathrm T\,\mathrm m$, respectively. This definition by itself does not assert that the limits exist.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: Radiation data, when they exist, are the uniform limits of $rE(rn,u+r/c)$ and $rB(rn,u+r/c)$ on compact retarded-time intervals. ([[def-emx-radiation-data]])

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and

$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by

most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

**Set form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), used to establish the Lebesgue measure space of [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), as carried by the surface-measure interface below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on the unit sphere $S^2\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), let $e_3:=(0,0,1)$ and write $n_3=n\cdot e_3$ for $n\in S^2$. Then:

(a) [Zonal identity] for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$, $$\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du.$$

(b) [Linear weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)\,f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3\int_{-1}^{1}u\,f(u)\,du.$$

(c) [Quadratic weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3^{2}\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du+\pi\,(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du.$$

(d) [Moments] $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, $\int_{S^2}n\,d\sigma=0$, $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=(4\pi/3)\delta_{ij}$, and for every $a\in\mathbb R^3$ $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2d\sigma=\frac{4\pi}{3}|a|^2,\qquad \int_{S^2}|n\times a|^2d\sigma=\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^2,$$ where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker symbol and $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(e) [Scope] (a)-(d) are identities for the polar surface measure of the unit sphere with only the stated continuity of $f$; they assert no physical field, flux or radiation statement. The measure is finite, so all displayed integrals are absolutely convergent; $f$ need not be nonnegative. For the uses on this page $f$ is a rational function with denominator bounded below by $1-b>0$, hence continuous on $[-1,1]$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $a,c,\mu_0>0$, let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^\infty$. Suppose $\rho(y,t)=J(y,t)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ and suppose the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=0$ holds everywhere.

Adopt the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations and the retarded, no-free-addition selection as the physical model assumptions. In the SI laboratory convention, define

$$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy.$$

The integrals converge absolutely at every $(x,t)$. The resulting potentials are jointly $C^\infty$ and satisfy $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$, and $\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Consequently $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ are jointly smooth and satisfy the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations for $(\rho,J)$ everywhere. This is the selected retarded solution, with no independent homogeneous field added. No compact support in time is assumed.

(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, with neighbourhoods as in
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and closure as in
[[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]].

- $x$ is an **adherent point** of $A$ when $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne
  \varnothing$ for every real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- $x$ is a **limit point** (or *accumulation point*) of $A$ when
  $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne \varnothing$ for every real
  $\varepsilon > 0$: every punctured neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$.
- $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ when $x \in A$ and there is a real
  $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$.
- The **derived set** of $A$ is
  $$A' \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \text{ is a limit point of } A \,\}.$$
- $A$ is **dense in $\mathbb{R}$** when $\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}$.

**A limit point is an adherent point**, since $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq
N_\varepsilon(x)$; and an element of $A$ is an adherent point of $A$, since
$x \in N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ ([[def-neighbourhood-r]]). So the adherent
points of $A$ are exactly the points of $A \cup A'$, a statement proved as part
of [[thm-closure-characterisations-r]].

**Limit point and isolated point are exact opposites inside $A$.** For
$x \in A$: $x$ is an isolated point of $A$ exactly when it is not a limit point
of $A$. Indeed $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$ says precisely that
$N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \varnothing$, because $x$ itself always lies in
$N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ when $x \in A$; so the existence of an $\varepsilon$
witnessing isolation is the negation of the condition defining a limit point.
A point of $A$ is therefore either isolated in $A$ or a limit point of $A$, and
never both.

**A limit point need not belong to the set, and a point of the set need not be a
limit point.** Both possibilities occur, and the two examples that matter later
are $0$, which is a limit point of $\{\, 1/k : k \ge 1 \,\}$ without belonging
to it, and $0$ again, which belongs to $\{0\} \cup [1,2]$ as an isolated point.

number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: Rationalizing the definition of $R$ gives $R(s)=\bigl((1-s/2)^2-(1-s)\bigr)/(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s}) =s^2/\bigl(4(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s})\bigr)$. The denominator is positive because $s<1$.

For real $a,b$, put $d:=a-b$ and $t:=d/2$. By [F3], $e^{ia}-e^{ib}=e^{ib}e^{it}(e^{it}-e^{-it})$. From the Euler formula and parity in [F2], $e^{-it}=\overline{e^{it}}$, so $e^{it}-e^{-it}=2i\sin t$; its modulus is $2|\sin t|$. By [F2] and [F6], the prefactor has modulus $|e^{ib}e^{it}|=|e^{ib}||e^{it}|=1$, and therefore $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|=2|\sin t|$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, with neighbourhoods as in
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and closure as in
[[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]].

- $x$ is an **adherent point** of $A$ when $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne
  \varnothing$ for every real $\varepsilon > 0$.
- $x$ is a **limit point** (or *accumulation point*) of $A$ when
  $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A \ne \varnothing$ for every real
  $\varepsilon > 0$: every punctured neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$.
- $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ when $x \in A$ and there is a real
  $\varepsilon > 0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$.
- The **derived set** of $A$ is
  $$A' \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \text{ is a limit point of } A \,\}.$$
- $A$ is **dense in $\mathbb{R}$** when $\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}$.

**A limit point is an adherent point**, since $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \subseteq
N_\varepsilon(x)$; and an element of $A$ is an adherent point of $A$, since
$x \in N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ ([[def-neighbourhood-r]]). So the adherent
points of $A$ are exactly the points of $A \cup A'$, a statement proved as part
of [[thm-closure-characterisations-r]].

**Limit point and isolated point are exact opposites inside $A$.** For
$x \in A$: $x$ is an isolated point of $A$ exactly when it is not a limit point
of $A$. Indeed $N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \{x\}$ says precisely that
$N^{*}_\varepsilon(x) \cap A = \varnothing$, because $x$ itself always lies in
$N_\varepsilon(x) \cap A$ when $x \in A$; so the existence of an $\varepsilon$
witnessing isolation is the negation of the condition defining a limit point.
A point of $A$ is therefore either isolated in $A$ or a limit point of $A$, and
never both.

**A limit point need not belong to the set, and a point of the set need not be a
limit point.** Both possibilities occur, and the two examples that matter later
are $0$, which is a limit point of $\{\, 1/k : k \ge 1 \,\}$ without belonging
to it, and $0$ again, which belongs to $\{0\} \cup [1,2]$ as an isolated point.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: On the punctured cap, the phase change $v_N=e^{i\sigma\phi}v_\sigma$ gives $A_N=A_\sigma-\sigma d\phi=\sigma(\cos\theta-1)d\phi$. Put $x=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$, and $z=\cos\theta$. Since $d\phi=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(1-z^2)$, this is $A_N=-\sigma(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(1+z)$, which extends smoothly across the north pole because $1+z>0$ there. The rephased frame itself also extends: for $\sigma=+1$ its components are $\frac{1}{2\sqrt2(1+z)}\bigl((1+z)^2-(x+iy)^2,\ i((1+z)^2+(x+iy)^2),\ -2(x+iy)(1+z)\bigr)^T$, and for $\sigma=-1$ they are the complex conjugates. These formulas have nonzero denominator throughout the north patch.

Along the loop, $\oint_\gamma A_N=\int_0^{2\pi}\sigma(\cos\theta_0-1)\,d\phi=-\sigma\Omega$, so [F1] gives $\mathrm{Hol}_\gamma=e^{-i\sigma\Omega}$. Direct integration of the global curvature over the north cap gives $\int_{\Sigma_N}F_\sigma=-\sigma\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=-\sigma\Omega$ as well. Thus the cap-flux expression agrees without using the singular spherical gauge at its pole.

In the spherical gauge, $\oint_\gamma A_\sigma=2\pi\sigma\cos\theta_0=-\sigma\Omega+2\pi\sigma$. Since $e^{i2\pi\sigma}=1$ for the integer helicities specified by [F1], exponentiation gives the same holonomy in both gauges.

$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

For the geometric initial-data convention, let $(M,g)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold and let $\iota:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedded three-manifold whose induced metric $h:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite. Its future unit normal $n$ satisfies $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,X)=0$ for $X\in T\Sigma$. The second fundamental form is $K(X,Y):=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$, with $\nabla$ the Levi-Civita connection of $g$ and the curvature sign convention stated in the Definition references section. The end data below are specified as a Riemannian metric and a symmetric tensor of these types; no embedding or Einstein constraint equation is required.

Let $E=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r>R_0\}$, where $R_0>0$ is a length, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ are Cartesian coordinates measured in metres, and $r:=\sqrt{(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2}$. Write $\delta:=\delta_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$ for the standard Euclidean metric, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise; repeated spatial indices are summed over $1,2,3$. A **fixed-chart asymptotically Euclidean end** consists of this exterior domain, a $C^2$ symmetric positive-definite covariant $2$-tensor $h=h_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$, and a $C^1$ symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $K=K_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$ such that
$$h_{ij}(x)=\delta_{ij}+\frac{a_{ij}}{r}+\rho_{ij}(x),\qquad K_{ij}(x)=O_1(r^{-2}),$$
where $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ is a constant real matrix, $\epsilon>0$, and $\rho=O_2(r^{-1-\epsilon})$. For any tensor components $T_{ij}$, the notation $T=O_k(r^{-q})$ means that for every multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ with $|\alpha|:=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3\le k$ there are constants $C_\alpha,R_\alpha$ such that $|\partial^\alpha T_{ij}(x)|\le C_\alpha r^{-q-|\alpha|}$ for $r\ge R_\alpha$, uniformly in angle. Thus the definition requires two Cartesian derivatives of the metric remainder and one of $K$. The coordinates and $r$ have units of metres; $\delta_{ij}$ and $h_{ij}$ are dimensionless, $a_{ij}$ has units of metres, and $K$ has inverse-length units in a spatial orthonormal frame.

For $R>R_0$, the coordinate sphere $S_R:=\{x:r=R\}$ is a smooth embedded surface in $E$. Let $\jmath_R:S_R\hookrightarrow E$ be its inclusion and $\gamma_R:=\jmath_R^*\delta$ its induced Riemannian metric. The Euclidean area measure $dS$ is the Riemannian area measure of $\gamma_R$: for any smooth rank-two local parametrization $X:U\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to S_R$ with coordinates $(y^1,y^2)$, its coordinate density is
$$dS=\sqrt{\det\bigl[\delta(\partial_{y^a}X,\partial_{y^b}X)\bigr]_{a,b=1}^{2}}\,dy^1dy^2.$$

The change-of-variables formula makes this density independent of the chosen surface coordinates; since $x$ is measured in metres, $dS$ has units of square metres. The sphere's outward Euclidean unit normal has components $n^i:=x^i/R$. If its limiting integral exists as $R\to\infty$—the spatial-infinity limit in this chosen chart—the **fixed-chart ADM energy** and its associated mass are
$$E_{\mathrm{ADM}}(h;x):=\frac{c^4}{16\pi G_N}\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}\bigl(\partial_jh_{ij}-\partial_ih_{jj}\bigr)n^i\,dS,\qquad M_{\mathrm{ADM}}:=\frac{E_{\mathrm{ADM}}}{c^2}.$$
Here $c>0$ is the SI speed-of-light conversion constant with units metres per second, and $G_N>0$ is the Newtonian gravitational conversion constant with units metres cubed per kilogram per second squared. The limit has units of metres, $E_{\mathrm{ADM}}$ has units of joules, and $M_{\mathrm{ADM}}$ has units of kilograms. The prefactor fixes the asymptotic time-translation normalization; in SI coordinates use $x^0=ct$. No rescaling of this convention is part of the definition.

derivations.claim: Set $w:=m/(2r)+\rho$. Derivatives of $r^{-1}$ satisfy $\partial^\alpha(r^{-1})=O(r^{-1-|\alpha|})$ for $|\alpha|\le2$, since each derivative is homogeneous of degree $-1-|\alpha|$ and bounded on the unit sphere. Together with $\rho=O_2(r^{-2})$, this gives $w=O_2(r^{-1})$; the product rule gives $w^2,w^3,w^4=O_2(r^{-2})$. Also $4w=2m/r+O_2(r^{-2})$, so the binomial expansion $u^4=(1+w)^4=1+4w+6w^2+4w^3+w^4$ yields $h_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+(2m\delta_{ij})/r+O_2(r^{-2})$. Since $u>0$, $h$ is positive definite and $C^2$, and the supplied symmetric $K$ is $C^1$ with $O_1(r^{-2})$ decay. Thus $(h,K)$ satisfies the definition of a fixed-chart end with $a_{ij}=2m\delta_{ij}$ and $\epsilon=1$. Now $h_{ij}=u^4\delta_{ij}$ gives $\partial_jh_{ij}=\partial_i(u^4)$ and $h_{jj}=3u^4$, hence $\partial_jh_{ij}-\partial_i h_{jj}=-2\partial_i(u^4)=-8u^3\partial_i u$. Contracting with $n^i=x^i/R$ on $S_R$ replaces $\partial_i u$ by $\partial_r u$.

The radial derivative bounds in [F1] and $\rho=O_2(r^{-2})$ give $u|_{S_R}=1+m/(2R)+O(R^{-2})$ and $\partial_r u|_{S_R}=-m/(2R^2)+O(R^{-3})$, uniformly in angle. Thus $u^3=1+O(R^{-1})$, so step 1.1's contracted integrand is $4m/R^2+O(R^{-3})$, uniformly on $S_R$.

Parameterize the complement of the poles and one meridian in $S_R$ by $X_R(\theta,\varphi)=R(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$, with coordinates $y^1=\theta\in(0,\pi)$ and $y^2=\varphi\in(0,2\pi)$. Its coordinate tangent vectors are $\partial_\theta X_R=R(\cos\theta\cos\varphi,\cos\theta\sin\varphi,-\sin\theta)$ and $\partial_\varphi X_R=R(-\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\sin\theta\cos\varphi,0)$, so the induced-metric Gram matrix is $[\delta(\partial_{y^a}X_R,\partial_{y^b}X_R)]_{a,b=1}^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}R^2&0\\0&R^2\sin^2\theta\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $R^4\sin^2\theta$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For the geometric initial-data convention, let $(M,g)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold and let $\iota:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$ be a smooth embedded three-manifold whose induced metric $h:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite. Its future unit normal $n$ satisfies $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,X)=0$ for $X\in T\Sigma$. The second fundamental form is $K(X,Y):=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$, with $\nabla$ the Levi-Civita connection of $g$ and the curvature sign convention stated in the Definition references section. The end data below are specified as a Riemannian metric and a symmetric tensor of these types; no embedding or Einstein constraint equation is required.

Let $E=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r>R_0\}$, where $R_0>0$ is a length, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ are Cartesian coordinates measured in metres, and $r:=\sqrt{(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2}$. Write $\delta:=\delta_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$ for the standard Euclidean metric, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise; repeated spatial indices are summed over $1,2,3$. A **fixed-chart asymptotically Euclidean end** consists of this exterior domain, a $C^2$ symmetric positive-definite covariant $2$-tensor $h=h_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$, and a $C^1$ symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $K=K_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j$ such that
$$h_{ij}(x)=\delta_{ij}+\frac{a_{ij}}{r}+\rho_{ij}(x),\qquad K_{ij}(x)=O_1(r^{-2}),$$
where $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ is a constant real matrix, $\epsilon>0$, and $\rho=O_2(r^{-1-\epsilon})$. For any tensor components $T_{ij}$, the notation $T=O_k(r^{-q})$ means that for every multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ with $|\alpha|:=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3\le k$ there are constants $C_\alpha,R_\alpha$ such that $|\partial^\alpha T_{ij}(x)|\le C_\alpha r^{-q-|\alpha|}$ for $r\ge R_\alpha$, uniformly in angle. Thus the definition requires two Cartesian derivatives of the metric remainder and one of $K$. The coordinates and $r$ have units of metres; $\delta_{ij}$ and $h_{ij}$ are dimensionless, $a_{ij}$ has units of metres, and $K$ has inverse-length units in a spatial orthonormal frame.

For $R>R_0$, the coordinate sphere $S_R:=\{x:r=R\}$ has outward Euclidean unit normal $n^i:=x^i/R$ and Euclidean area measure $dS$. If its limiting integral exists as $R\to\infty$—the spatial-infinity limit in this chosen chart—the **fixed-chart ADM energy** and its associated mass are
$$E_{\mathrm{ADM}}(h;x):=\frac{c^4}{16\pi G_N}\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}\bigl(\partial_jh_{ij}-\partial_ih_{jj}\bigr)n^i\,dS,\qquad M_{\mathrm{ADM}}:=\frac{E_{\mathrm{ADM}}}{c^2}.$$
Here $c>0$ is the SI speed-of-light conversion constant with units metres per second, and $G_N>0$ is the Newtonian gravitational conversion constant with units metres cubed per kilogram per second squared. The limit has units of metres, $E_{\mathrm{ADM}}$ has units of joules, and $M_{\mathrm{ADM}}$ has units of kilograms. The prefactor fixes the asymptotic time-translation normalization; in SI coordinates use $x^0=ct$. No rescaling of this convention is part of the definition.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Fix one evolution problem, its state space and its declared classical solution class. For the general-relativity application here, use one fixed periodic symmetric-hyperbolic system on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ with integer regularity $s\ge5$, a fixed coordinate gauge and reconstruction, smooth coefficient maps on an open state domain $O$, symmetric principal matrices and a positive time matrix. The relevant fixed-gauge context is the one defined by `def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology`: one coefficient family and one matter branch, compact state sets $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, a uniform positive lower and finite upper bound for $A^0$ on $K_2$, and separate bounds $R_z,R_t$ for the state and its time derivative. The state components are divided by their fixed unit scales before their Euclidean-valued Sobolev norms are formed; these are coordinate norms and do not quotient by diffeomorphisms. On each compact time slab, the resulting normalized state $u$ belongs to $L^\infty H^s\cap C^0H^{s-1}$ and has $\partial_tu\in L^\infty H^{s-1}$.

A forward solution is given on $[0,T_{\max})$, where $T_{\max}\in(0,\infty]$. It is **maximal** in this solution class if, when $T_{\max}<\infty$, no solution on $[0,T_{\max}+\rho)$ for any $\rho>0$ agrees with it on $[0,T_{\max})$. Let $E_{\rm raw}$ be a specified nonnegative scalar functional of the solution, continuous on every compact subinterval of $[0,T_{\max})$. If $E_{\rm raw}$ has physical units, choose a fixed positive scale $E_*$ with the same units and set $E=E_{\rm raw}/E_*$. If $E_{\rm raw}$ is dimensionless, set $E=E_{\rm raw}$. In either case $E$ is dimensionless. In the general-relativity convention the time coordinate is $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ in metres; choose a fixed length scale $L_*>0$ and use the dimensionless time $t=x^0/L_*$. Thus $\partial_t=L_*\partial_{x^0}$. The fixed-gauge bound $R_t$ is on $\partial_{x^0}u$ and has units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding bound with respect to $t$ is $L_*R_t$. The constants $A$, $\epsilon$ and $\eta$ below are dimensionless as well. In a purely mathematical application, take these variables as real scalars without a physical interpretation.

Specify a finite list of dimensionless margin functions $m_j:[0,T_{\max})\to\mathbb R$ and thresholds $\mu_j>0$. Write $\mathcal M(T)$ when $m_j(t)\ge\mu_j$ for every listed $j$ and every $0\le t<T$. The **continuation criterion** is a separate result for the chosen evolution problem: if a solution has a finite right endpoint $T$ with $E(t)\le\eta$ for every $0\le t<T$ and $\mathcal M(T)$, then it extends past $T$ in the same solution class.

For constants $A>0$, $\epsilon>0$ and $\eta>0$ with $2A\epsilon^2<\eta$, a **bootstrap estimate** is the implication, required on every finite $T<T_{\max}$,

$$\left[ E(t)\le2A\epsilon^2\text{ for all }0\le t\le T\right]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left[ E(t)\le A\epsilon^2\text{ for all }0\le t\le T\right].$$

This contract records the continuity and continuation inputs needed by an application. It does not itself prove the bootstrap estimate, the margin bounds, or any Einstein evolution estimate.

Let a solution of a fixed evolution problem be maximal on $[0,T_{\max})$ and satisfy the preceding continuation and bootstrap contract, with its constants $A,\epsilon,\eta$ and initial bound $E(0)<A\epsilon^2$. If the bootstrap improvement holds on every compact subinterval, then $E(t)\le A\epsilon^2$ for all $t<T_{\max}$. If the listed margins persist throughout the interval, then $T_{\max}=\infty$.

derivations.claim: On any finite $[0,T]$, set $u=E$, $a(t)=E_0$ and $b(t)=C\epsilon(1+t)^{-1-\delta}$. These functions satisfy [F1]'s continuity and nonnegativity hypotheses, and $a$ is nondecreasing. Therefore $E(t)\le E_0\exp\!\left(C\epsilon\int_0^t(1+s)^{-1-\delta}\,ds\right)$.

For $t=0$ the integral is zero. For $t>0$, the function $G(s)=-\delta^{-1}(1+s)^{-\delta}$ has derivative $G'(s)=(1+s)^{-1-\delta}$ by [F3] and [F4]; $G'$ is continuous on $[0,T]$. Applying [F5] gives $\int_0^t(1+s)^{-1-\delta}\,ds=\delta^{-1}[1-(1+t)^{-\delta}]$. By [F2] and [F6], $(1+t)^{-\delta}>0$, so the exponent $q(t):=\frac{C\epsilon}{\delta}[1-(1+t)^{-\delta}]$ satisfies $q(t)\le C\epsilon/\delta$. By [F7], $\exp(q(t))\le\exp(C\epsilon/\delta)$; since $C\epsilon/\delta>0$, [F7] and [F8] give $\exp(C\epsilon/\delta)>1$. As $E_0\ge0$, these inequalities prove both displayed bounds and $E_0\le E_0\exp(C\epsilon/\delta)$.

If additionally $E_0e^{C\epsilon/\delta}<A\epsilon^2$, the bound in step 2.1 implies $E(t)<A\epsilon^2$ on every compact interval and $E(0)\le E_0<A\epsilon^2$. Thus the strict improvement required by the contract holds whenever its hypothesis $E\le2A\epsilon^2$ holds. With the separately supplied margins, [F10] then yields the conditional continuation conclusion; the scalar calculation itself proves no such margins.

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

For every admissible integer $N\ge3$, time-step count $n_{\max}\ge1$, real
step $k>0$, and pair of real periodic input arrays, the algorithm terminates
after exactly $n_{\max}-1$ update passes and outputs all levels through
$u^{n_{\max}}$. In the unit-cost exact-real-arithmetic model, where each scalar
arithmetic operation and each array read or write has bounded cost independent
of $N$ and $n_{\max}$, its operation count is $O(Nn_{\max})$.

Let $N\ge3$, $h=2\pi/N$, $k>0$, and $\lambda=k/h$. Complexify the real
linear recurrence of the periodic wave algorithm. For each discrete Fourier
index $\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ define the mode
$$
e_\ell(j):=\exp(2\pi i\ell j/N),\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
$$
If $0<\lambda<1$, every nonconstant mode ($\ell\ne0$) has recurrence
coefficient
$$
c_\ell:=1-2\lambda^2\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)\in(-1,1)
$$
and two distinct amplification roots
$$
z_{\ell,\pm}:=c_\ell\pm i\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2},\qquad |z_{\ell,\pm}|=1.
$$
Consequently, each fixed nonconstant mode has bounded amplitude on every
finite slab. For arbitrary real initial arrays define their spatial means by
$$
\bar u^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u^0_j,\qquad \bar v^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}v^0_j.
$$
The constant mode has the repeated root $1$ and evolves exactly as
$\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$; for any fixed $T\ge0$ it is bounded on the slab
$0\le nk\le T$ but has no uniform-in-time displacement bound when
$\bar v^0\ne0$. This statement
does not assert that the condition $0<\lambda<1$ alone proves convergence of a
numerical relativity scheme. Define the nonzero discrete frequencies $\omega_\ell:=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$. On this fixed torus they satisfy the mesh-independent lower bound
$$\omega_\ell\ge\frac2\pi\qquad(N\ge3,\ 1\le\ell<N).$$
In particular each fixed grid has a positive minimum. This frequency bound is not a mesh-independent amplitude bound for arbitrary unscaled two-step data $(a_0,a_1)$: the distinct-root coefficients in the mode solution can depend on the grid and the initial data. The constant-mode qualifications above are unchanged.
For even $N$, the alternating mode with Fourier index $\ell=N/2$ is called
the Nyquist mode. At the endpoint $\lambda=1$, if $N$ is even and
$u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$, $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ for real amplitudes $a_0,\beta_0$,
then each output level satisfies
$$
u_j^n=(-1)^j(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0).
$$
The Nyquist amplification root is repeated at $-1$, and a nonzero Nyquist
