Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Because $N$ is even, both periodic neighbors of $(-1)^j$ equal $-(-1)^j$. Hence $(D_hu^0)_j=-4h^{-2}(-1)^j$, and the startup in [F1] gives $a_0=1$ and $a_1=1-2(k/h)^2=c$. This mode has index $\ell=N/2$; it is outside the strict range of [F3].

The two roots $z_{\rm grow}=c-r$ and $z_{\rm decay}=c+r$ satisfy $z_{\rm grow}z_{\rm decay}=1$; also $z_{\rm grow}<-1$ and $z_{\rm decay}=1/z_{\rm grow}\in(-1,0)$.

The sequence $(z_{\rm grow}^n+z_{\rm decay}^n)/2$ satisfies the recurrence because each root satisfies $z^2-2cz+1=0$, and its values at $n=0,1$ are $1,c$. Induction identifies it with $a_n$. For even $n$ the two powers are nonnegative, and for odd $n$ they are both negative; since $1/2>0$, their half-sum has the same sign. The piecewise definition [F5] therefore gives $|a_n|=(|z_{\rm grow}^n|+|z_{\rm decay}^n|)/2$, while induction using multiplicativity [F6] gives $|z_{\rm grow}^n|=|z_{\rm grow}|^n$ and $|z_{\rm decay}^n|=|z_{\rm decay}|^n$. Since $z_{\rm grow}<-1$, [F5] gives $|z_{\rm grow}|=-z_{\rm grow}>1$, while $|z_{\rm decay}|^n\ge0$ by [F6]; hence $|a_n|\ge|z_{\rm grow}|^n/2$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $N\ge3$, $h=2\pi/N$, $k>0$, and $\lambda=k/h$. Complexify the real
linear recurrence of the periodic wave algorithm. For each discrete Fourier
index $\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ define the mode
$$
e_\ell(j):=\exp(2\pi i\ell j/N),\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
$$
If $0<\lambda<1$, every nonconstant mode ($\ell\ne0$) has recurrence
coefficient
$$
c_\ell:=1-2\lambda^2\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)\in(-1,1)
$$
and two distinct amplification roots
$$
z_{\ell,\pm}:=c_\ell\pm i\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2},\qquad |z_{\ell,\pm}|=1.
$$
Consequently, each fixed nonconstant mode has bounded amplitude on every
finite slab. For arbitrary real initial arrays define their spatial means by
$$
\bar u^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u^0_j,\qquad \bar v^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}v^0_j.
$$
The constant mode has the repeated root $1$ and evolves exactly as
$\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$; for any fixed $T\ge0$ it is bounded on the slab
$0\le nk\le T$ but has no uniform-in-time displacement bound when
$\bar v^0\ne0$. This statement
does not assert that the condition $0<\lambda<1$ alone proves convergence of a
numerical relativity scheme. For each fixed $N$, define the nonzero discrete
frequencies $\omega_\ell:=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$.
This finite list has a positive minimum; it is a fixed-grid fact and no bound
uniform in $N$ is asserted.
For even $N$, the alternating mode with Fourier index $\ell=N/2$ is called
the Nyquist mode. At the endpoint $\lambda=1$, if $N$ is even and
$u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$, $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ for real amplitudes $a_0,\beta_0$,
then each output level satisfies
$$
u_j^n=(-1)^j(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0).
$$
The Nyquist amplification root is repeated at $-1$, and a nonzero Nyquist
velocity amplitude $\beta_0$ gives linear growth in the step number.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad
\omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad
F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold, let $U\subseteq M$ be open, and let
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ be the dual coframe of a smooth
future-directed tetrad on $U$. Let $\omega^I{}_J$ be a smooth matrix-valued
one-form with $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J=-\omega_{JI}$, and let
$\nabla$ be its induced affine connection as in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Then

$$de^I+\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J=0\quad\text{for every }I$$

if and only if $\nabla$ is torsion-free. There is exactly one such
$\eta$-skew connection: the Levi-Civita connection of $g$. Under a smooth
change $e'=\Lambda e$, $\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$, the torsion and curvature
forms obey

$$T'=\Lambda T,\qquad F'=\Lambda F\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented and
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let
$P^+_g(M)$ be its smooth oriented time-oriented orthonormal frame bundle from
[[prop-gr-fx-oriented-time-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]]. Set
$\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3):=SL(2,\mathbb C)$ and let
$\rho:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to SO^+(1,3)$ be the Hermitian-matrix covering
homomorphism of [[prop-gr-fx-spin-double-cover]]. A **Lorentzian spin
structure** is a smooth right principal $SL(2,\mathbb C)$-bundle
$\widetilde P\to M$ together with a smooth map $\lambda:\widetilde P\to
P^+_g(M)$ over the identity of $M$ such that

$$\lambda(ua)=\lambda(u)\rho(a)\qquad (u\in\widetilde P,\ a\in SL(2,\mathbb C)),$$

and the restriction of $\lambda$ to each fiber is a surjective two-sheeted
covering map. The map is over the identity, meaning $\pi^+\circ\lambda=\widetilde\pi$; the square below displays this base condition and is not used as a proof.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
\widetilde P \arrow[r,"\lambda"] \arrow[d,"\widetilde\pi"'] & P^+_g(M) \arrow[d,"\pi^+"] \\
M \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}_M"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

A smooth finite-dimensional complex representation here consists of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_\sigma$ and a smooth group
homomorphism $\sigma:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to GL(V_\sigma)$, where
$GL(V_\sigma)$ is the group of invertible complex-linear maps on
$V_\sigma$, with the smooth structure inherited as an open subset of the
real vector space of complex-linear endomorphisms of $V_\sigma$. Its
**associated vector bundle** is the quotient
$$\widetilde P\times_\sigma V_\sigma:=(\widetilde P\times V_\sigma)/\sim,$$
where $\sim$ is the equivalence relation generated by
$(ua,v)\sim(u,\sigma(a)v)$ for $u\in\widetilde P$,
$a\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$ and $v\in V_\sigma$; equivalently
$(u,v)\sim(ua,\sigma(a)^{-1}v)$, in the convention of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]. Write $[u,v]$ for
the class of $(u,v)$. Since every $\sigma(a)$ is complex-linear, the
fiberwise vector-space operations
$[u,v]+[u,w]=[u,v+w]$ and $z[u,v]=[u,zv]$ for $z\in\mathbb C$ are
independent of the representative. The associated-bundle proposition
[[prop-associated-bundle-is-locally-trivial-and-functorial-under-pullback]]
gives local triviality; on an overlap with local sections satisfying
$s_j(x)=s_i(x)a_{ij}(x)$, the smooth principal charts give transition maps
$(x,v)\mapsto(x,\sigma(a_{ij}(x))v)$. These are smooth because $\sigma$ is
smooth and define the smooth vector-bundle structure. When $V_\sigma$ is
chosen for spinor components, this is called its associated spinor bundle.
With the defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$ chosen for spinor
components, it is a rank-two complex spinor bundle.

To define a **lift of a Lorentz connection**, first supply a principal
connection $H^+\subset TP^+_g(M)$ on the frame bundle: it is a smooth vector
subbundle complementary to $VP^+:=\ker(d\pi^+)$ and invariant under the
right $SO^+(1,3)$ action, as in
[[def-principal-connection-and-vertical-curvature]]. This $H^+$ is additional
global data; the local affine connection and local matrix $\omega$ in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]] do not determine it unless they are
specified as restrictions of a chosen global metric-compatible affine
connection whose induced principal connection is the supplied $H^+$. A lift
is a supplied principal connection $\widetilde H\subset T\widetilde P$,
likewise a smooth
right-invariant horizontal complement to
$V\widetilde P:=\ker(d\widetilde\pi)$, such that
$d\lambda_u(\widetilde H_u)=H^+_{\lambda(u)}$ at each
$u\in\widetilde P$. It induces a covariant derivative on the associated
vector bundle by horizontal differentiation: a section is represented by a
smooth equivariant map $f:\widetilde P\to V_\sigma$ with
$f(ua)=\sigma(a)^{-1}f(u)$, and its derivative along a smooth base vector
field $X$ at $x$ is the class $[u,df_u(\widetilde X^H_u)]$ for
$u\in\widetilde P_x$, where $\widetilde X^H$ is the horizontal lift. The local
Clifford-compatibility calculation is a separate proposition about supplied
gamma matrices and does not follow from the existence of $\sigma$ alone.
A spin structure, a global spinor field, and a lifted connection are extra data: this definition asserts
neither existence nor uniqueness of a spin lift, global tetrad, or connection
lift. The matrix group and covering homomorphism are Lorentzian; the Euclidean
$\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ cover is not substituted.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the cited smooth Lie-group convention. For a complex matrix $A$, write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. Let
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and define
$SL(2,\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det A=1\}$. Let
$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and
$X(x)=x^0I+x^1\sigma_1+x^2\sigma_2+x^3\sigma_3$ for
$x\in\mathbb R^4$. The real-linear map $x\mapsto X(x)$ identifies
$\mathbb R^4$ with the Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices and
$-\det X(x)=-(x^0)^2+(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2$. For $A\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$,
let $\rho(A)$ be the real linear transformation defined by

$$X(\rho(A)x)=AX(x)A^\dagger.$$

Then $\rho:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to SO^+(1,3)$ is a smooth surjective Lie-group
homomorphism, its kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$, and its differential at the
identity is an isomorphism. In particular, $\rho$ is a two-sheeted covering
homomorphism. This is a local group statement; it does not assert that a
spacetime admits a global spin lift.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold, let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Let
$\nabla$ be a smooth affine Lorentz connection on $TM|_U$ with smooth
connection matrix $\omega^I{}_J$ in $E$, meaning
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$ as in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Write
$\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J=-\omega_{JI}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so $\eta^{IJ}$ denotes the entries of
$\eta^{-1}=\eta$. Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and constant
matrices $\gamma^I\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfying

$$\gamma^I\gamma^J+\gamma^J\gamma^I=2\eta^{IJ}I_n.$$

Let $V\in\Gamma^\infty(TM|_U)$ be a smooth vector field and let
$\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb C^n)$ be smooth. With $V_I:=\eta_{IJ}V^J$,
define $c(V):=V_I\gamma^I$ and, on $\mathbb C^n$-valued fields and forms,

$$D\psi:=d\psi+\Gamma\psi,\qquad \Gamma:=\frac14\omega_{IJ}\gamma^I\gamma^J,$$

where $d$ acts componentwise. Then

$$D(c(V)\psi)=c(\nabla V)\psi+c(V)D\psi,$$

where $(\nabla V)_I:=dV_I-\omega^J{}_I V_J$ are the covector components
of the induced Lorentz connection and $c(\nabla V):=(\nabla V)_I\gamma^I$.
This is precisely a local matrix identity under the stated hypotheses; it
does not assert that the matrices $\gamma^I$ or the operator $D$ are
compatible with, or induced by, a separately supplied $SL(2,\mathbb C)$
representation or principal-connection lift. Such compatibility is an
additional condition when this identity is used to describe an associated
spinor bundle.

derivations.claim:
Put $c=\cosh r$ and $s=\sinh r$. Multiplying the upper-left $2\times2$ block gives
$B(r)^{\mathsf T}\eta B(r)=\eta$, because $c^2-s^2=1$ and the off-diagonal time-space terms cancel. The determinant of that block is $1$, the remaining block is identity, and $B(r)e_0=(c,s,0,0)$ is future timelike since $c>|s|$. Hence $B(r)\in SO^+(1,3)$. For the Euclidean form, however,
$\delta(B(r)e_0,B(r)e_0)=c^2+s^2>1=\delta(e_0,e_0)$ for $r\ne0$, so $B(r)\notin SO(4)$. A map with codomain $SO(4)$ cannot lift this element through its covering map.

Write $A(r)=\cosh(r/2)I+\sinh(r/2)\sigma_1$. Its eigenvalues are $e^{r/2}$ and $e^{-r/2}$, so $\det A(r)=1$. Pauli multiplication gives
$AIA^\dagger=\cosh r\,I+\sinh r\,\sigma_1$,
$A\sigma_1A^\dagger=\sinh r\,I+\cosh r\,\sigma_1$, and
$A\sigma_jA^\dagger=\sigma_j$ for $j=2,3$; thus its Hermitian action is exactly $B(r)$. By [F4] it is the Lorentzian spin lift, consistent with the target group in [F3].

On the Cartesian tetrad $e^I=dx^I$, $de^I=0$, so $\omega=0$ gives zero torsion and is $\eta$-skew. By [F2] it induces the unique Levi-Civita connection. The boost $B(r)$ is constant on spacetime, so $e' =B(r)e$ also has $de' =0$ and its transformed connection is $\omega'=0$ by [F1]; the torsion remains zero. The local matrix identity from [F5] uses the same $\eta$; it does not identify this operator as one induced by a group representation. Thus neither the Euclidean metric nor its compact spin group supplies this Lorentzian interface.

Let $M_2(\mathbb C)$ have its Euclidean topology as $\mathbb R^8$, write $Q^\dagger:=\overline Q^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and define

$$SU(2)=\{Q\in M_2(\mathbb C):Q^\dagger Q=I_2,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

Under matrix multiplication, $SU(2)$ is a compact Hausdorff topological group.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ and $\sigma:G\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ be
finite-dimensional complex representations of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Their
**tensor product representation** $\rho\otimes\sigma$ is the representation of
$G$ on the complex tensor product $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ given on elementary
tensors by

$$g\cdot(v\otimes w):=\bigl(\rho(g)v\bigr)\otimes\bigl(\sigma(g)w\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ v\in V,\ w\in W).$$

**The action is well defined.** For fixed $g\in G$, the assignment
$(v,w)\mapsto\rho(g)v\otimes\sigma(g)w$ is additive in each variable and
$\mathbb C$-balanced, because $\rho(g)$ and $\sigma(g)$ are $\mathbb C$-linear:
$\rho(g)(v\lambda)\otimes\sigma(g)w=(\rho(g)v)\lambda\otimes\sigma(g)w$. By
[[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]] there is a unique
$\mathbb C$-linear map $\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g):V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W\to
V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ with the displayed value on every elementary tensor.
Because the two sides of
$g\cdot(h\cdot(v\otimes w))=(gh)\cdot(v\otimes w)$ agree on every elementary
tensor and the elementary tensors span $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$, the assignment
$g\mapsto\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g)$ is a group homomorphism into
$\operatorname{GL}(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)$, with
$\rho(1)\otimes\sigma(1)=\operatorname{id}$. The underlying space is
finite-dimensional: bases of $V$ and $W$ give the basis
$(v_i\otimes w_j)_{i,j}$, so $\dim(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)=(\dim V)(\dim W)$.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional complex
representation of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Its
**dual** or **contragredient** representation is the representation $\rho^{*}$
of $G$ on the algebraic dual space $V^{*}$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]) defined by

$$\bigl(g\cdot f\bigr)(v):=f\bigl(g^{-1}\cdot v\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ f\in V^{*},\ v\in V),$$

equivalently $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$.

Each operator $\rho^{*}(g)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear because $f$ and
$\rho(g^{-1})$ are. The inverse appears so that composition is
order-preserving: writing $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$,

$$(gh)\cdot f=f\circ\rho\bigl((gh)^{-1}\bigr)=f\circ\rho(h^{-1})\circ\rho(g^{-1})=g\cdot(h\cdot f),$$

and $1\cdot f=f\circ\operatorname{id}_V=f$. Hence $\rho^{*}$ is a group
homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V^{*})$, a representation of the same
degree as $\rho$.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $G$ be a topological group and $H$ a complex Hilbert space. A
**unitary representation** of $G$ on $H$ is a group homomorphism
$\pi:G\to U(H)$, where $U(H)$ is the group of bijective complex-linear
isometries of $H$, such that the orbit map $g\mapsto\pi(g)v$ is norm-continuous
for every $v\in H$. This condition is **strong continuity**. A closed linear
subspace $M\subseteq H$ is **invariant** if $\pi(g)M=M$ for every $g\in G$.
The representation is **irreducible** if $H\ne\{0\}$ and its only closed
invariant linear subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $H$.

For unitary representations $\pi$ on $H$ and $\rho$ on $K$, a **bounded
intertwiner** is a bounded linear operator $T:H\to K$ satisfying
$$T\pi(g)=\rho(g)T\qquad(g\in G).$$
The representations are **unitarily equivalent** if there is a unitary
intertwiner between them. The **commutant** of $\pi$ is
$$\pi(G)'=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):T\pi(g)=\pi(g)T\text{ for every }g\in G\}.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]). Under the assumed
Axiom of Choice the Axiom of Countable Choice holds as well
([[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]]).

Let $\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]),
and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). The pairing below is linear in the first
variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

**The scalar integrals.** Fix $v\in H$ and $w\in J$ and put

$$b_v(w):=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k).$$

The integrand is continuous on $K$. Indeed, $k\mapsto T\pi(k)^{-1}v$ is
continuous because $\pi$ is strongly continuous and $T$ is bounded, and for a
continuous map $\psi$ into $J$ the map $k\mapsto\sigma(k)\psi(k)$ is continuous
because every $\sigma(k)$ is an isometry: for fixed $k_0$,

$$\|\sigma(k)\psi(k)-\sigma(k_0)\psi(k_0)\|\le\|\psi(k)-\psi(k_0)\|+\|(\sigma(k)-\sigma(k_0))\psi(k_0)\|,$$

and both terms tend to zero as $k\to k_0$. A continuous complex function on the
compact space $K$ is bounded and Borel, so the displayed integral is a finite
complex number; and $\bigl|\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\bigr|\le
\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$ for every $k$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]), so
$|b_v(w)|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$. For fixed $v$ the assignment
$w\mapsto b_v(w)$ is conjugate-linear and $\|w\|\mapsto\|b_v(w)\|$ is bounded
by $\|T\|\,\|v\|$; hence

$$\varphi_v(w):=\overline{b_v(w)}=\int_K\langle w,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$

is a bounded linear functional on $J$ of norm at most $\|T\|\,\|v\|$.

**The definition.** Under Countable Choice the Hilbert space $J$ has the Riesz
representation property ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]): there
is a unique vector $A(T)v\in J$ with $\varphi_v(w)=\langle w,A(T)v\rangle$ for
every $w\in J$, equivalently

$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=b_v(w)=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)\qquad(v\in H,\ w\in J).$$

This determines $A(T)$ as a map $H\to J$, the **Haar average** of $T$ with
respect to the pair $(\sigma,\pi)$.

**Well-definedness.** For each $v$ the vector $A(T)v$ is unique, so $A(T)$ is a
well-defined function. It is linear: if $v=a v_1+b v_2$ then, by the
conjugate-linearity in $f$ of the representing vector recorded in
[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]], the vector representing
$\varphi_{av_1+bv_2}=\overline a\,\varphi_{v_1}+\overline b\,\varphi_{v_2}$ is
$aA(T)v_1+bA(T)v_2$; and $\|A(T)v\|=\|\varphi_v\|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|$ because the
Riesz representation is isometric, so $A(T)$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$. The assignment $A$ is itself linear in $T$: for fixed $v,w$
the integrand is linear in $T$, so the scalar integral is, and equality of the
weak matrix elements together with uniqueness of the Riesz vector gives
$A(aT+bT')=aA(T)+bA(T')$. Thus
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ is a well-defined map.

**This is a weak operator integral.** Only scalar functions are integrated in
the definition: for fixed $v$ and $w$, the continuous function
$k\mapsto\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle$ is integrated against the
scalar measure $\mu$, and the vector $A(T)v$ is then produced by the Riesz
representation theorem. No operator-norm continuity of the orbit
$k\mapsto\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}$ of an arbitrary bounded operator $T$ is assumed
or asserted. For finite-rank $T:H\to J$, it follows from
[[lem-conjugation-orbits-of-finite-rank-operators-are-norm-continuous]] as
follows. Equip $H\oplus J$ with the sum inner product; it is a Hilbert space
because Cauchy sequences converge in each coordinate. The representation
$\tau(k)(v,w)=(\pi(k)v,\sigma(k)w)$ is unitary and strongly continuous.
The bounded finite-rank operator $S(v,w)=(0,Tv)$ satisfies
$\tau(k)S\tau(k)^{-1}(v,w)=(0,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v)$.
The cited lemma makes this conjugation orbit norm continuous, and restriction
to $H\oplus\{0\}$ followed by projection onto $J$ does not increase operator
norm, proving the claimed continuity for $T$. Only
the Axiom of Choice is used, through normalized Haar measure and Countable
Choice. That $A$ is an idempotent contraction onto the bounded intertwiners,
with operator norm one exactly when $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, is the
content of [[lem-haar-averaging-projects-onto-the-intertwiner-space]], which
justifies the present definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]), and let
$\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]).
Write
$$\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J):=\{T\in\mathcal B(H,J):T\pi(g)=\sigma(g)T\text{ for every }g\in K\}$$
for the space of bounded intertwiners and let
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ be the Haar averaging operator of
[[def-haar-averaging-operator-on-hom-spaces]], so that
$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$
for all $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$, $v\in H$, $w\in J$. Then:

1. $A$ is idempotent, $A\circ A=A$, and its range is exactly
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)$: $A(T)$ intertwines for every bounded $T$, and
   $A(T)=T$ for every bounded intertwiner $T$;
2. $A$ is a contraction, $\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$ for every $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$,
   hence $\|A\|\le1$;
3. $\|A\|=1$ if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, and $\|A\|=0$ if
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)=\{0\}$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem (For a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space, $V=W\oplus W^\perp$) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: For each dual factor, choose an orthonormal basis of $V_e$ and use its dual-basis inner product; this is basis-independent because a change between orthonormal bases preserves the Euclidean coefficient norm. The matrix of the dual action is the transpose of the inverse unitary matrix, hence is unitary. Tensor products of orthonormal bases are an orthonormal basis for the displayed tensor inner product, so the diagonal action is unitary by [F3]–[F4]. Its matrix entries are finite sums and products of continuous entries of the edge representations, so [F7] makes $R_v$ strongly continuous.

For fixed $w\in W_v$, define $T_w:\mathbb C\to W_v$ by $T_w(z)=zw$, with the trivial representation on $\mathbb C$. It is linear and bounded by [F8], with $\|T_w\|=\|w\|$. The intertwining equation $T_w(z)=R_v(g)T_w(z)$ for all $z$ is equivalent to $w\in W_v^{SU(2)}$.

By [F1], $SU(2)$ is compact Hausdorff; by [F2] and [F5], its normalized Haar probability exists under the stated full AC assumption. The hypotheses of [F9]–[F10] now hold for $H=\mathbb C$, $J=W_v$, and $T=T_w$, using [F6], [F7], and steps 1.1 and 2.1. Since the trivial representation acts as the identity, the weak Haar average of $T_w$ is $T_{P_vw}$, where the finite-dimensional vector integral is defined coordinatewise. The range clause of [F10] therefore gives $P_v^2=P_v$, $\|P_v\|\le1$, and $\operatorname{ran}P_v=W_v^{SU(2)}$.

If $x\in\operatorname{ran}P_v$ and $y\in\ker P_v$, then $P_v(x+ty)=x$ for every complex scalar $t$. Contractivity gives $\|x\|\le\|x+ty\|$. Squaring and taking real $t$ of both signs forces $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=0$; taking $t$ purely imaginary of both signs forces $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=0$. Hence range and kernel are orthogonal. Since an idempotent has $W_v=\operatorname{ran}P_v\oplus\ker P_v$, the kernel is the orthogonal complement of the range, and [F11] identifies $P_v$ as the orthogonal projection onto its invariant range.

On $W=\bigotimes_vW_v$, each vertex operator acts as $P_v$ on one factor and identity on the others. Operators on distinct tensor factors commute, so their product is an idempotent whose range is $\bigotimes_v\operatorname{ran}P_v$, the tensors invariant under every vertex action. It is the orthogonal projection onto this joint invariant subspace because tensor products of orthogonal projections are orthogonal projections in the product Hilbert structure. If the graph has no vertices, the empty product is the identity on $\mathbb C$, consistent with the statement.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ and let $H_{\mathrm{pp}}$,
$H_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ be the subspaces of
[[def-pure-point-absolutely-continuous-and-singular-continuous-spectral-subspaces]].
Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually
orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with
$$H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}},$$
canonically determined by $T$; the restrictions of $T$ to them are
self-adjoint and their spectral measures are respectively purely atomic,
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and atomless and
singular. If $H$ is separable and $\mu$ is a maximal scalar spectral measure
with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$
of its discrete, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, then
$H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.

Here a support means a Borel carrier (zero mass off the set), not necessarily topological support. A maximal scalar spectral measure is a finite positive Borel measure mu with $E_x\ll\mu$ for every x (in particular a scalar spectral measure with this domination property qualifies). The last assertion is conditional on the supplied mu. On the zero Hilbert space use the unique PVM and full-domain zero operator directly.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $\epsilon>0$, and define $\mathcal F_\epsilon$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by [[def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner]]. It extends uniquely to a unitary operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For $Z=(q,p)$, define the normalized Gaussian packet $$ g_Z^\epsilon(x):=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}e^{ip\cdot(x-q/2)/\epsilon}. $$ Its norm is $1$ by [F3] at zero after applying [F9] to the translation and positive scaling of the nonnegative Gaussian. For $u\in\mathcal S$, put $V_\epsilon u(Z)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle$. The Fourier transform of the shifted Gaussian gives $$ \langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}(2\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}\mathcal F_\epsilon\!\left(u(\,\cdot\,)e^{-|\cdot-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}\right)(p). $$ Plancherel [F2], followed by Tonelli [F4] and the Gaussian integral from [F3] after [F9], gives $$ \|V_\epsilon u\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int|\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle|^2\,dq\,dp=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int\!\!\int |u(x)|^2e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dx\,dq=\|u\|_2^2. $$ The middle equality follows from Plancherel [F2] for each fixed $q$; the final equality uses the Gaussian integral [F3] in $q$, with Tonelli [F4]. The same identity holds for all $u\in L^2$ by [F2] and Tonelli [F4]. Polarization gives $\langle u,v\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle\overline{\langle v,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle}\,dZ$, hence the weak resolution $$ u=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle g_Z^\epsilon\,dZ . $$

For $u\in\mathcal S$, the joint function $F(x,q):=u(x)e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,q)$: each derivative is a finite sum of derivatives of $u$, Gaussian factors, and polynomials in $x-q$, and the inequality $\langle q\rangle^m\le C_m\langle x\rangle^m\langle x-q\rangle^m$ transfers every $q$-weight to a Schwartz factor and a Gaussian moment. Its partial Fourier transform in $x$ is Schwartz in $(p,q)$ by the same full Fourier/inverse Fourier argument as [F8]. The additional phase $e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}$ in $\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle$ has derivatives that are polynomial factors, so the packet coefficient $V_\epsilon u$ remains Schwartz in $Z=(q,p)$. The Schwartz seminorms of $Z\mapsto g_Z^\epsilon$ grow at most polynomially in $Z$, so the resolution integral in step 1.1 converges in every Schwartz seminorm. The product $u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,y)$; its partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F8], so $\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\in\mathcal S$ and $|B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\le\|a\|_\infty\|\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\|_1$ proves continuity of the form in Schwartz seminorms. If $a\in\mathcal S$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz; the kernel pairing is absolutely convergent, and the change $q=(x+y)/2,\ r=x-y$, followed by $r\mapsto-y$, identifies it with $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)$. Thus the bounded-symbol form extends the kernel definition on Schwartz symbols. Applying the continuous form to the two Schwartz-convergent resolutions is valid; Fubini [F5] for the resulting absolutely integrable products gives $$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\iint B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon)V_\epsilon u(Z')\overline{V_\epsilon v(Z)}\,dZ'\,dZ . $$

Let $Z=(q,p)$, $Z'=(q',p')$, $m=(Z+Z')/2$, and $\delta=Z-Z'$. Define $\sigma((x,\xi),(x',\xi'))=x\cdot\xi'-\xi\cdot x'$. Substitution of the packets into $\mathcal W_\epsilon[g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon]$, completing the square in $y$, and applying [F3] gives $$ \mathcal W_\epsilon[g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon](z)=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d}e^{-|w|^2/\epsilon}e^{-i\sigma(w,\delta)/\epsilon+i	heta(Z,Z')},\qquad w=z-m, $$ with $|e^{i	heta(Z,Z')}|=1$. If $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$, its $L^1$ norm is $1$, hence $|B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq\|a\|_\infty$. If $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$, then $$ L_\delta:= rac{\epsilon}{i|\delta|^2}
abla_w\phi_\delta\cdot
abla_w,\qquad \phi_\delta(w):=-\sigma(w,\delta) $$ satisfies $L_\delta e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}=e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}$, since $|
abla_w\phi_\delta|=|\delta|$. Integrating by parts $N_d$ times against the Gaussian is justified coordinatewise by [F10] and Fubini [F5]: derivatives of the Gaussian are integrable, derivatives of $a$ are bounded, and the Gaussian forces the endpoint products to vanish. Translation $w=z-m$ and scaling $w=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ in these absolutely integrable terms are justified by [F9]. Each derivative on the Gaussian contributes a factor bounded by $\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$; a derivative on $a$ contributes $\epsilon/|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$, since $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\leq1$. Thus $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq C_d\left(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\epsilon^{|\alpha|/2}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\inftyight)(1+|\delta|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}\leq C_dD(a)(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}, $$ where $D(a)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty$. Increasing $C_d$ makes this bound valid also when $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$.

Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. The same holds with $Z,Z'$ interchanged. Thus the integral kernel $$ K_\epsilon(Z,Z'):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon) $$ has uniformly bounded row and column $L^1$ norms, each at most $C_dD(a)$. For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$, Tonelli [F4] and the column bound show that $\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2dZ'$ is finite for almost every $Z$. For each such $Z$, write $$ \int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'=\int\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\,\frac{K_\epsilon(Z,Z')}{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|}f(Z')\,dZ', $$ using quotient $0$ where $K_\epsilon=0$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] in $L^2(dZ')$ yields $$ |\int K_\epsilon(Z,Z')f(Z')\,dZ'|^2\leq(\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')|\,dZ')\int|K_\epsilon(Z,Z')||f(Z')|^2\,dZ'. $$ Integrating in $Z$ and using Tonelli [F4] and the column bound yields $\|K_\epsilon f\|_2\leq C_dD(a)\|f\|_2$. Applying this estimate to step 2.1 and using the isometry in step 1.1 proves $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\leq C_dD(a)\|V_\epsilon u\|_2\|V_\epsilon v\|_2=C_dD(a)\|u\|_2\|v\|_2 . $$

For fixed $u\in\mathcal S$, the bounded form in step 3.1 extends continuously in $v$ to $L^2$, which is a Hilbert space by [F6], and $v\mapsto\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}$ is a bounded linear functional there. Riesz representation [F7] gives a unique $y\in L^2$ with $\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}=\langle v,y\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$; conjugate symmetry gives $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=\langle y,v\rangle$, so set $A_\epsilon u=y$. Its norm is at most $C_dD(a)\|u\|_2$. Uniqueness makes $u\mapsto A_\epsilon u$ linear on $\mathcal S$, and [F11] makes its extension to all of $L^2$ unique. Hence the operator norm is at most $C_dD(a)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

Assume full AC. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ rank-one orthogonal projection family. Let $E_P$ be its complex line bundle, $\nabla=P\,d$, and $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
For any $C^2$ closed path $\gamma$ subdivided into local unit frames $u_j$, with $A_j=u_j^*du_j$ and transition $u_{j+1}=u_jg_j$ for $g_j$ valued in $U(1)$ at the crossing points, the holonomy is the scalar by which parallel transport acts on its one-dimensional initial fiber. This scalar is the product of the local factors $\exp(-\int_{\gamma_j}A_j)$ and the transition factors $g_j^{-1}$. Thus geometric holonomy includes the frame-transition scalars whenever one frame does not cover the path.

In addition, suppose $\Sigma=\Sigma_N\cup\Sigma_S$ is a decomposition into compact oriented subsurfaces with disjoint interiors and common finite boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Sigma_N=-\partial\Sigma_S$, a finite union of oriented smooth circles. If $E_P$ has supplied $C^2$ unit frames $u_N,u_S$ on these subsurfaces and $u_S=u_Ng$ on $\Gamma$ for a $C^2$ map $g:\Gamma\to U(1)$, then
$$\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle=\operatorname{wind}(g):=\sum_{\Gamma_j\subset\Gamma}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma_j}g^{-1}dg\in\mathbb Z,$$
where each component $\Gamma_j$ has the orientation induced by $\partial\Sigma_N$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

Assume full AC. Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ have its outward area form $\omega$. Let $D^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|\leq1\}$ have orientation $dx\wedge dy$; $C^2$ maps on $D^2$ have derivatives through order two extending continuously to the boundary. Set
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_+(n)=\frac{I+n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z}{2}.$$
For any two $C^2$ maps $f_0,f_1:D^2\to S^2$ from an oriented disk, with the same boundary map and its induced boundary orientation, the two oriented solid-angle integrals differ by a multiple of $4\pi$:
$$\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega\in4\pi\mathbb Z.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Matrix multiplication gives $(n\cdot\sigma)^*=(n\cdot\sigma)$ and $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=I$, while $\operatorname{tr}(n\cdot\sigma)=0$. Hence $P_+^*=P_+^2=P_+$ and $\operatorname{tr}P_+=1$, so it is a rank-one orthogonal projection. Direct multiplication gives $(n\cdot\sigma)u_N=u_N$ and $u_N^*u_N=1$, so $u_N$ is a normalized local frame of its positive eigenline.

Differentiating the displayed spinor gives $u_N^*du_N=i\sin^2(\theta/2)\,d\phi=i(1-\cos\theta)d\phi/2$. Taking the exterior derivative yields $dA_N=i\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi/2$, which is the curvature in this frame by [F1]. Both the projector curvature and the spherical area form are global smooth two-forms, so their equality on the northern chart gives $F=(i/2)\omega_{S^2}$ globally.

Integrating the area form gives $\int_{S^2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi$, hence $\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}F=\frac{i}{2\pi}\frac{i}{2}(4\pi)=-1$. By [F2] this is the integral first Chern number with the stated anti-Hermitian connection convention.

A southern frame is $u_S=(e^{-i\phi}\cos(\theta/2),\sin(\theta/2))^T=e^{-i\phi}u_N$; it is regular at the south pole and together with $u_N$ covers $S^2$. Along the equator the transition is $g(\phi)=e^{-i\phi}$, so $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}g^{-1}dg=-1$. The two-hemisphere clutching clause in [F2] therefore gives Chern number $-1$, matching the direct curvature integral in step 3.1 and fixing the orientation sign. Pull these frames back to the standard closed parameter disk filling $S$. Their inverse images form an open cover of the disk; by [F5] it has a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. Choose $N$ with $\sqrt2/N<\delta$, set $h=1/N$, and intersect the disk with the closed axis-aligned squares $[ih,(i+1)h]\times[jh,(j+1)h]$. Retain only intersections $C_{ij}$ with nonempty interior. There are finitely many; their interiors are disjoint and their closures cover the disk, since every disk point is a limit of interior points off the grid lines and a subsequence lies in one of finitely many retained cells. Each cell has diameter at most $\sqrt2h<\delta$, so it lies in one frame patch. Each is a compact convex region whose boundary, after zero-length pieces are discarded, is a finite union of regular straight or circular arcs meeting at finitely many corners; the C1 Stokes item [F3] applies. On a cell $C_{ij}$, its frame connection $A_{ij}$ is $C^1$ because the filling is $C^2$, and [F3] gives $\int_{\partial C_{ij}}A_{ij}=\int_{C_{ij}}F$. Since one frame covers the cell, its boundary holonomy is $\exp(-\int_{\partial C_{ij}}A_{ij})=\exp(-\int_{C_{ij}}F)$. Choose a unit vector at each vertex of this finite cell decomposition and write each oriented edge transport as its unit-modulus scalar in those endpoint vectors. In the product of the cell-boundary holonomies every internal edge occurs once in each direction, so its scalar and inverse cancel; only the outer boundary loop remains. Thus $\operatorname{Hol}(C)=\exp(-\int_SF)=\exp(-i\Omega/2)$. If a second filling is chosen, [F4] says its solid angle differs by $4\pi k$ for some integer $k$, so this exponential is independent of the filling. For a latitude circle the north-cap integral is $\Omega=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\theta\sin u\,du\,d\phi=2\pi(1-\cos\theta)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.
