derivations.claim: For each connected component $K_j$, start with any flat assignment and set the root gauge value at $v_j$ to the identity. Along the unique tree paths in $T_j$ from $v_j$, choose the gauge value at each new vertex so that the transformed label on the traversed tree edge is the identity; when that edge is traversed against its chosen orientation, use its inverse label. This recursively produces a tree-normalized assignment on every component. It is unique among gauges whose value at each $v_j$ is the identity, since the condition that each transformed tree label remain $1$ determines each next vertex value.

In a tree-normalized assignment on $K_j$, every edge of $T_j$ has label $1$. Assign to each generator $x_e$ of $\pi_1(K_j,v_j)$ the inverse of the label on its oriented non-tree edge. By [F4], this is a homomorphism for the traversal-first product on loops: holonomy of a concatenation is the reverse-ordered product, and reversing the path in the Statement reverses that order. Flatness says exactly that every relator $r_f$ maps to $1$. By the presentation in [F2], the normalized assignments on $K_j$ are in bijection with homomorphisms $\rho:\pi_1(K_j,v_j)\to G$.

For a connected subcomplex $L_i\subseteq K_{j(i)}$ and base data as in the Statement, the pointed inclusion at $v_i$ induces a well-defined homomorphism on fundamental groups by [F5]. The base-path change map $c_{\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}:\pi_1(K_{j(i)},v_i)\to\pi_1(K_{j(i)},w_{j(i)})$, given by $[\alpha]\mapsto[\gamma_i*\alpha*\bar\gamma_i]$, is a well-defined isomorphism: endpoint-fixed homotopies remain endpoint-fixed after adjoining $\gamma_i,\bar\gamma_i$, insertion of the retraced path $\bar\gamma_i*\gamma_i$ contracts in a product of loop classes, and $c_{\bar\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}$ is its inverse. Thus $\iota_{\gamma_i,*}=c_{\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}\circ\iota_*$ is well defined. For a flat assignment $A$ and an edge loop $\ell$ in $L_i$, the edge-product convention gives $\Phi_{K_{j(i)}}(A)(\iota_{\gamma_i,*}[\ell])=H_A(\bar\gamma_i)H_A(\bar\ell)H_A(\gamma_i)=H_A(\bar\gamma_i)\Phi_{L_i}(A|_{L_i})([\ell])H_A(\bar\gamma_i)^{-1}$. If a gauge arrow $h:A\to A'$ is applied, its path-product rule gives $H_{A'}(\bar\gamma_i)=h(w_{j(i)})H_A(\bar\gamma_i)h(v_i)^{-1}$; this is exactly the naturality condition for the stated conjugation arrows. Hence inverse path holonomy intertwines restriction with the componentwise precomposition functor up to that natural isomorphism.

On a fixed component $K_j$, a gauge transformation taking one tree-normalized assignment to another must have equal values at the two endpoints of every edge of $T_j$, because both edge labels are $1$. Since $T_j$ is connected, it is constant on all vertices of $K_j$. Conversely, each constant gauge value $a\in G$ preserves tree normalization and conjugates every generator label by $a$. Thus the full subgroupoid on tree-normalized objects over $K_j$ is identified with $\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K_j,v_j),G)//G$. Step 1.1 makes its inclusion into the full flat-connection groupoid essentially surjective, and the inclusion is fully faithful because it is full. The root-one gauge used in step 1.1 leaves inverse path holonomy at $v_j$ unchanged, so the object map $\Phi_{K_j}$ in the Statement agrees with normalization followed by this identification. For any gauge arrow $h:A\to A'$, the gauge factors telescope along each based edge loop $\delta$ at $v_j$ to give $H_{A'}(\bar\delta)=h(v_j)H_A(\bar\delta)h(v_j)^{-1}$, so $\Phi_{K_j}(A')=h(v_j)\Phi_{K_j}(A)h(v_j)^{-1}$. Conversely, after normalizing $A$ and $A'$ by root-one gauges, each conjugating arrow between their representations is the unique constant gauge arrow between the normalized assignments; conjugating back gives the unique gauge arrow between $A$ and $A'$ with that value at $v_j$. Hence the stated functor is fully faithful as well as essentially surjective, and is an equivalence.

For each connected component $K_j$, the subgroup of vertex gauges equal to $1$ at $v_j$ acts freely and transitively on each fiber of the map from flat assignments to their tree-normalized representative, by step 1.1 and its uniqueness. Its order is $|G|^{|(K_j)_0|-1}$, so $|\operatorname{Flat}(K_j,G)|=|G|^{|(K_j)_0|-1}|\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K_j,v_j),G)|$. Substituting this count into [F1] gives the connected normalization. Equivalently, the action-groupoid cardinality in step 3.1 sums $1/|\operatorname{Stab}(\rho)|$ over conjugacy classes; no freeness of the conjugation action is assumed.

For $K=K_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup K_m$, the defining edge-label and vertex-gauge data split componentwise, so $\mathcal C_G(K)=\prod_j\mathcal C_G(K_j)$. Applying step 3.1 on each component gives the product equivalence $\Phi_K:\mathcal C_G(K)\simeq\mathcal R_G(K)$, and applying step 2.2 componentwise gives the stated restriction naturality. Automorphism orders multiply in a product groupoid and its isomorphism classes are componentwise tuples, so its groupoid cardinality is the product of the connected cardinalities from step 4.1. When $m=0$, the empty product is terminal with cardinality $1$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**Setting.** Fix $n\ge2$ and the two graded additive monoidal categories of this
page: the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, the idempotent completion of
the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]), and the Karoubi envelope
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ of the type-A diagrammatic category
$D$ ([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]).
Both are graded: an object $X$ has a shift $X(1)=X\{-1\}$, and both are monoidal
with unit the one-object bimodule $R$ respectively the empty word. Both are
additive in the sense of [[def-additive-category]].

**The split Grothendieck group.** For such a category $C$ choose a *small
skeleton*, that is, a set $\operatorname{sk}(C)$ of representative objects
meeting every isomorphism class exactly once — for $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ one may take
the graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules with a fixed underlying set of words, and for
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ the idempotents in finite direct sums of shifts of words,
so that the representatives form a set rather than a proper class. Define
$$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C):=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{X\in\operatorname{sk}(C)}\mathbb Z[X]\Bigr)\Big/\,\bigl\langle[X]-[X']-[X'']\ :\ X\cong X'\oplus X''\ \text{in }C\bigr\rangle,$$
the free abelian group on the isomorphism classes of representative objects

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The setting.** Keep $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_i=2$, the
place-permutation action of $S_n$, the balanced roots
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$ with $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$ and the
graded $(R,R)$-bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]; recall that
$1\otimes1\in B_i$ has degree $-1$ and $1\otimes\alpha_i$ has degree $1$, that
$B_i$ is generated as an $(R,R)$-bimodule by $1\otimes1$, and that $R=R^{s_i}\oplus\alpha_iR^{s_i}$ with
$s_i(\alpha_i)=-\alpha_i$
([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]],
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]).

**The positive generator complex.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ let $F_i$ be the
bounded cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i:=\bigl[\;B_i\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_i\ }R(1)\;\bigr],$$
with $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$, $R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and
all other terms zero, where $\varepsilon_i:B_i\to R(1)$ is the
multiplication map $\varepsilon_i(r\otimes r')=rr'$, i.e. the degree-zero
bimodule map determined by $\varepsilon_i(1\otimes1)=1$ and
$\varepsilon_i(1\otimes\alpha_i)=\alpha_i$.

**The negative generator complex.** Let $F_i^{-1}$ be the bounded cochain
complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules
$$F_i^{-1}:=\bigl[\;R(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta_i\ }B_i\;\bigr],$$
with $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$, $B_i$ in cohomological degree $0$ and
all other terms zero, where $\eta_i:R(-1)\to B_i$ is the bimodule map
$\eta_i(1)=\alpha_i\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_i$.

**Well-definedness of the differentials.** The map $\varepsilon_i$ descends
from the multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$ because
$\varepsilon_i(ra\otimes r')=rar'=\varepsilon_i(r\otimes ar')$ for $a\in R^{s_i}$
and $R$ is commutative; it is left and right $R$-linear and homogeneous of
degree zero, since $1\otimes1\mapsto1$ matches the degrees $-1$ of $B_i$ and of
the generator of $R(1)$, and $1\otimes\alpha_i\mapsto\alpha_i$ matches the
degree $1=\deg(\alpha_i)-1$ on both sides. For $\eta_i$, the bimodule map
$R\to B_i$ sending $1$ to the class of $x_i-x'_{i+1}$ is well defined: the
products $(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_i-x'_i)$ and
$(x_i-x'_{i+1})(x_{i+1}-x'_{i+1})$ vanish in $B_i$ by the explicit computation
of GKS Lemma 3.8, while for $a\notin\{i,i+1\}$ the factor $x_a-x'_a$ is already
a defining relation of $B_i$, so the element annihilates the kernel ideal of the
multiplication $R\otimes_{\mathbb Q}R\to R$, and the assignment $1\mapsto x_i-x'_{i+1}$
extends to a well-defined $R$-bimodule map. The value of that map at $1$ times
the unit $2\varepsilon_i$ is $\eta_i(1)$, because
$$1\otimes(x_i-x_{i+1})+(x_i-x_{i+1})\otimes1=2(x_i-x'_{i+1})$$
in $B_i$ (GKS Lemma 3.8, using $x_i+x_{i+1}=x'_i+x'_{i+1}$) and
$\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$; a unit multiple of a well-defined
bimodule map is a well-defined bimodule map, so $\eta_i$ is well defined. Its
value $\eta_i(1)$ is homogeneous of degree $1$, matching the degree of
$1\in R(-1)$, so $\eta_i$ is a degree-zero bimodule map. Both complexes are
concentrated in two adjacent cohomological
degrees, so $d^2=0$ holds trivially and each of $F_i,F_i^{-1}$ is a bounded
cochain complex of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules in the sense of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]].

**Size and consequences.** The bimodules $R$, $R(1)$ and $R(-1)$ are free of
rank one on both sides and $B_i$ is free of rank two on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]], the bases
being $\{1\otimes1,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ on the left and
$\{1\otimes1,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ on the right). Every term of $F_i$ and of
$F_i^{-1}$ is therefore finite free, hence finite graded projective, as a left
$R$-module and as an underlying right $R$-module. Applying
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]]
with the commutative ring $\mathbb Q$ and $A=B=R$: the signed totalization with
$F_i$ is an exact triangulated functor on bounded complexes of finite graded
projective $R$-modules, preserves quasi-isomorphisms between bounded complexes,
and descends to the derived tensor functor $F_i\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}-$ on
$D^b(R\text{-grmod})$; the same statements hold with $F_i^{-1}$ in place of
$F_i$. The right-tensor construction $-\otimes_RF_i$ is defined separately by
signed totalization, and its derived version uses the same two-sided
freeness. Commutativity of $R$ does not assert a symmetry between tensor
products of arbitrary $(R,R)$-bimodules.

**Recorded convention.** The complex $F_i$ is the library normalization of
Rouquier's positive complex $F_s=[A\otimes_{A^s}A\to A]$, in which $A$ sits in
degree $1$ and the differential is multiplication: in the library external
shift $(r)$ with $M(r)_d=M_{d+r}$ one has $F_i=T_i(1)$ and
$F_i^{-1}\cong T_i^{-1}(-1)$ for the GKS complexes
$T_i=[B_i(-1)\to R]$, $T_i^{-1}=[R\to B_i(1)]$ of formula (3.3). The GKS negative differential sends $1$ to
$x_i-x'_{i+1}$, whereas ours is $2\varepsilon_i$ times that map.
The chain isomorphism $F_i^{-1}\to T_i^{-1}(-1)$ is multiplication by
$2\varepsilon_i$ in degree $-1$ and the identity in degree $0$.
The internal shifts cancel in inverse pairs and agree on the two sides of
each positive braid relation. The sign $\varepsilon_i$
in $\alpha_i=\varepsilon_i(x_i-x_{i+1})$, and with it the sign of $\eta_i$, is
a unit of $\mathbb Q$; the homotopy classes of the complexes do not depend on
the choice of balanced root.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

**Convention for comparison.** The library's positive generator $F_i$ is
Rouquier's $F_{s_i}=[A\otimes_{A^{s_i}}A\to A]$ with the library external shift
$(1)$ on both terms, after giving the polynomial variables degree $2$:
$$F_i=[(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)(1)\longrightarrow R(1)].$$
Rouquier's negative complex of §3.2.4 becomes $F_i^{-1}$ after doubling
internal degrees and shifting the whole complex by $(-1)$, up to the unit
scalar coming from the root normalization. As recorded in
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], the
complexes of Rouquier, Gorsky–Kivinen–Simental, Khovanov and Elias–Krasner
differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
comparison with those sources is read through the dictionary recorded there.
The empty word corresponds to the trivial braid and to the identity functor.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $t,u$ be signed words for the same braid $v$. Then the normalized map
$$\gamma_{t,u}\colon F(t)\longrightarrow F(u)$$
of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]
is a canonical homotopy equivalence, natural with respect to the multiplication
maps: for every other braid $v'$ with chosen words $t',u'$, the diagrams
comparing $F(t)\otimes_RF(t')$ with $F(u)\otimes_RF(u')$ commute up to the
canonical associativity isomorphisms, and $\gamma_{t,u}$ is the unique homotopy
class with the prescribed derived image $c_{t,u}$. Consequently the object
$G_v$ of [[thm-rouquier-complexes-form-a-coherent-braid-group-action]] is
independent of the chosen representative up to canonical homotopy equivalence,
and the notation $F(\beta)$ for the Rouquier complex of a braid element is well
defined up to canonical isomorphism in $K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$; this is an
isomorphism statement in the homotopy category, not an equality of complexes.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For every braid $v\in B_n$ choose a signed word $t(v)$ representing it, taking
$t(1)$ to be the empty word, and put $G_v:=F(t(v))$, with $G_1:=R$. For
the action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$, set $F_1=\operatorname{Id}$ and, for
$v\ne1$, set $F_v:=G_v\otimes_R-$. For
$v,w\in B_n$ let
$$m_{v,w}\colon G_v\otimes_RG_w\longrightarrow G_{vw}$$
be the unique homotopy class whose derived image is the graph-multiplication
comparison, transported through the associativity and unit isomorphisms of
[[thm-bounded-bimodule-tensor-associativity-unit-and-cone-compatibility]];
equivalently $m_{v,w}$ is $\gamma_{t(v)t(w),\,t(vw)}$ in the normalization of
[[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]. Let
$m_1\colon G_1\to R$ be the identity of the unit complex. For $v,w\ne1$, the
compositor $\mu_{v,w}:F_vF_w\Rightarrow F_{vw}$ is induced by associating
$G_v\otimes_R(G_w\otimes_R-)$ to $(G_v\otimes_RG_w)\otimes_R-$ and then
applying $m_{v,w}\otimes_R-$, followed by the left-unit identification
$R\otimes_R-\cong\operatorname{Id}$ when $vw=1$. If either index is $1$, use
the canonical tensor unit identifications, so the compositor is the identity
after those identifications; set $u:F_1\Rightarrow\operatorname{Id}$ to the
identity.
Then $(F_v,\mu_{v,w},u)$ is a coherent action of $B_n$ on
$K^b(R\text{-grmod})$ in the sense of
[[def-coherent-action-of-a-group-on-a-category]]: the functors are the exact
left tensor functors $G_v\otimes_R-$ for $v\ne1$, with the identity functor at
$1$, and both composites of every pentagon have the same derived image,
namely the same associative graph multiplication, so the pentagon commutes by
uniqueness in degree $0$; both unit triangles hold by the canonical tensor
unit identifications. Equivalently, $v\mapsto(F_v,\mu_{v,w},u)$ is a monoidal
functor from the discrete strict monoidal category $(B_n,\cdot)$ to the strict
monoidal category of endofunctors of $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$. The construction
uses one chosen word per braid and no other choice; no choice principle is
needed.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d\geq1$, let spins be $s_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, let $h_i\in\mathbb R$, and let $J_{ij}=J_{ji}\in\mathbb R$ with $J_{ii}=0$ and $J_{ij}=0$ whenever $\|i-j\|_\infty>R$ for some finite integer $R$. No translation invariance is assumed. For finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and exterior $\eta\in\{-1,+1\}^{\Lambda^c}$, define $\widehat s_i=s_i$ on $\Lambda$ and $\widehat s_i=\eta_i$ outside, and use
$$E_\Lambda(s_\Lambda\mid\eta)=-\sum_{\{i,j\}:\{i,j\}\cap\Lambda\ne\varnothing}J_{ij}\widehat s_i\widehat s_j-\sum_{i\in\Lambda}h_i s_i,$$
where the pair sum is over unordered distinct pairs and is finite by the range assumption. For site $i$ and exterior spins $\eta\in\{-1,+1\}^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}$, the one-site law is explicitly
$$\gamma_i(s\mid\eta)=\frac{\exp\!\left(\beta\left[h_i s+\sum_{k\ne i}J_{ik}s\eta_k\right]\right)}{\sum_{u\in\{-1,+1\}}\exp\!\left(\beta\left[h_i u+\sum_{k\ne i}J_{ik}u\eta_k\right]\right)},\qquad s\in\{-1,+1\};$$
the sums are finite by the range condition. For $i\ne j$, define
$$c_{ij}:=\sup_{\eta,\eta':\,\eta_k=\eta'_k\ (k\ne j)}\frac12\sum_{s\in\{-1,+1\}}|\gamma_i(s\mid\eta)-\gamma_i(s\mid\eta')|,\qquad c_{ii}:=0.$$
Then $c_{ij}=0$ if $J_{ij}=0$, and otherwise
$$c_{ij}\leq\tanh(\beta|J_{ij}|).$$
In particular, $\sup_i\sum_j\tanh(\beta|J_{ij}|)<1$ is a sufficient Dobrushin row-sum bound for every bounded field profile $(h_i)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\gamma$ and $\widetilde\gamma$ be proper consistent finite-range specifications on $X$, each with a uniform finite one-site influence radius. Finite range means that for every finite $\Delta$ and cylinder event $A$, each function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_A\mid\eta)$ and $\eta\mapsto\widetilde\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_A\mid\eta)$ depends on only finitely many exterior coordinates, as in [[def-csm-lattice-gibbs-specification]]. For each $i,j\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_{ii}=0$ and let $C_{ij}\geq0$ dominate both Dobrushin coefficients $c^\gamma_{ij}$ and $c^{\widetilde\gamma}_{ij}$ of [[def-csm-frontier-dobrushin-matrix]]. Assume $C_{ij}=0$ whenever $\lVert i-j\rVert_\infty>R$ for some finite integer $R\geq0$ and assume

$$\sup_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}C_{ij}\leq c<1.$$

For each site $i$, define the one-site conditional discrepancy

$$b_i:=\sup_{\eta\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}}\lVert\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)-\widetilde\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)\rVert_{\rm TV}.$$

Write $C_\Lambda=(C_{ij})_{i,j\in\Lambda}$ and $D^\Lambda:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty C_\Lambda^n$ for finite $\Lambda$, with $C_\Lambda^0$ the identity matrix on $\Lambda$; also write $D_{ij}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(C^n)_{ij}$ for the infinite-lattice resolvent entries. These sums are finite entrywise, because every row sum of $C^n$ and $C_\Lambda^n$ is at most $c^n$. A cylinder function is one depending only on the spins in some finite set. For a bounded real cylinder function $f:X\to\mathbb R$, define its oscillation by $\delta_i(f):=\sup_{\sigma,\sigma':\,\sigma_k=\sigma'_k\ (k\ne i)}|f(\sigma)-f(\sigma')|$; only finitely many $\delta_i(f)$ are nonzero.

For every nonempty finite $\Lambda$ containing a finite coordinate set $K_f$ on which $f$ depends, and exterior configurations $\xi,\zeta\in S^{\Lambda^c}$, the corresponding finite-volume Gibbs distributions satisfy

$$|\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\xi)-\widetilde\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\zeta)|\leq\sum_{i\in\Lambda}\delta_i(f)\sum_{k\in\Lambda}D^\Lambda_{ik}\left(b_k+\sum_{j\notin\Lambda}C_{kj}\mathbf1_{\{\xi_j\ne\zeta_j\}}\right).$$

Moreover, each specification has a unique DLR state, denoted $\mu$ and $\widetilde\mu$, and every bounded real cylinder function satisfies

$$|\mu(f)-\widetilde\mu(f)|\leq\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}\delta_i(f)\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}D_{ij}b_j.$$

In particular, when $\gamma=\widetilde\gamma$ the comparison bound is zero. The estimates are conditional mathematical consequences of the stated finite-spin specifications and strict row bound.

derivations.claim: For each site $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, the condition $\lVert i-j\rVert_1=1$ holds for exactly $2d$ distinct sites $j$. By [F1], each of these coefficients is at most $\tanh(\beta|J|)$ and all remaining coefficients vanish, so $\sum_jc_{ij}\leq2d\tanh(\beta|J|)$ for every $i$.

If $2d\tanh(\beta|J|)<1$, the displayed influence row bound is strict. For two specifications with the same nearest-neighbor coupling magnitude and different finite field profiles, the same coefficient bound holds for each, so their pointwise maximum is a common envelope with row sum below $1$. By [A1], the hypotheses of [F2] are met, yielding the comparison estimate. The inequality is only sufficient; it makes no claim that failure of the bound entails nonuniqueness.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: If $u=0$, then $h(q)=0$ forces $q(1)=0$ and $q(0)=1$, so the constraint fiber is the singleton $(0,1)$. By [F1], $D((0,1)\|p)=\ln2$, and therefore $s(0)=-\ln2=H_2(0)-\ln2$. If $0<u\leq1$, then $h(q)=u$ forces $q(1)=u^4$ and $q(0)=1-u^4$, again a singleton fiber. The relative-entropy formula in [F1] gives $D(q\|p)=u^4\ln(2u^4)+(1-u^4)\ln(2(1-u^4))=\ln2-H_2(u^4)$; hence $s(u)=H_2(u^4)-\ln2$.
For $0<u<1$, [F4]–[F5] give $H_2'(x)=\ln((1-x)/x)$ and therefore $s'(u)=4u^3\ln((1-u^4)/u^4)$. Differentiating once more yields $s''(u)=u^2 B(u)$, where $B(u):=12\ln((1-u^4)/u^4)-16/(1-u^4)$.

On $0<u\leq1/9$, $R(u):=(1-u^4)/u^4=u^{-4}-1$ decreases and $1/(1-u^4)$ increases, so $B(u)$ decreases. At $u=1/9$, $R(u)=6560$ and $B(1/9)=12\ln6560-16\cdot6561/6560$. Since $6560>16$, [F3] gives $\ln6560>\ln16=4\ln2$; and [F4] gives $\ln2=\int_1^2dt/t>1/2$ because $1/t\geq1/2$ on $[1,2]$ with strict inequality on $[1,2)$. Thus $12\ln6560>24$. Also $16\cdot6561/6560<17$ by integer multiplication, so $B(1/9)>7$ and $B(u)>0$ throughout $(0,1/9]$. In particular $s''(u)>0$ on that interval. By applying [F6] first to $s'$ and then to $s$, positive second derivative makes $s'$ strictly increasing and every interior chord lie strictly above the graph; hence $s$ is strictly convex on $(0,1/9)$.

Fix $u\in(0,1/10]$ and choose $t>0$ so that $0<u-t<u+t<1/9$, possible because $1/10<1/9$. Strict convexity from step 3.1 gives $s(u-t)+s(u+t)>2s(u)$. If an upper supporting line with slope $\beta$ existed at $u$, its inequalities at $u-t$ and $u+t$ would instead give $s(u-t)+s(u+t)\leq[s(u)-\beta t]+[s(u)+\beta t]=2s(u)$, a contradiction. By [F2], no such energy is canonical for any real $\beta$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be a nonempty finite set, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$ with nonnegative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums, and let $\nu$ be an initial probability vector. Then there exists a uniformized realization under the conventions stated below. Its paths are càdlàg and almost surely have only finitely many event times on each bounded interval (nonexplosion), and, for all $0\le s\le t$,
$$\mathbb P(X_t=j\mid\mathcal F_s)=(e^{(t-s)L})_{X_sj}\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is the construction filtration. In particular, $e^{tL}$ is the transition matrix from any initial state.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be finite and nonempty, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$, let $X$ be its uniformized realization from the preceding existence result, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Put $g=Lf$ and
$$M_t=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t g(X_s)\,ds,\qquad \Gamma_f(i)=L(f^2)(i)-2f(i)Lf(i).$$For every finite $T$, $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is a square-integrable martingale relative to the construction filtration, and$$A_t:=\int_0^t\Gamma_f(X_s)\,ds$$
is its continuous predictable bracket: $A_0=0$, $A$ is increasing and predictable, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale. The bracket is understood in the continuous predictable increasing compensator convention stated in the proof.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

derivations.claim: For fixed $s$, reindexing the bond sum as in the model generator gives $L_NF_s^N(\eta)=\langle\pi^N(\eta),\Delta_NH(s,\cdot)\rangle$; also $\partial_sF_s^N(\eta)=\langle\pi^N(\eta),\partial_sH(s,\cdot)\rangle$. Hence the compensating drift in the Statement is exactly $(\partial_sF_s^N+L_NF_s^N)(\eta_s)$.

Fix $N$ and a state $i=\eta_s$. By [F2], on an interval of length $h$, two or more potential uniformization events have probability $O_N(h^2)$, one actual transition $i\to j$ has probability $hL_N(i,j)+O_N(h^2)$, and no state change has probability $1-h\lambda_i+O_N(h^2)$, with $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_N(i,j)$. Taylor expansion is uniform over the finite state set and $s\in[0,T]$. If no state change occurs, then $F_{s+h}^N(i)-F_s^N(i)=h\partial_sF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$ and the compensating integral is $h(\partial_sF_s^N+L_NF_s^N)(i)+O_N(h^2)$, so the increment of $M^N$ is $-hL_NF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$. A single transition $i\to j$ gives increment $F_s^N(j)-F_s^N(i)+O_N(h)$; summing its conditional mean over $j$ gives $hL_NF_s^N(i)+O_N(h^2)$, which cancels the no-transition term. Paths with at least two potential events contribute $O_N(h^2)$ because $M^N$ has bounded increments for fixed $N,T$. Therefore $|\mathbb E[M_{s+h}^N-M_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]|\le C_Nh^2$. In the conditional second moment, no transition contributes $O_N(h^2)$, one transition contributes $h\sum_{j\ne i}L_N(i,j)(F_s^N(j)-F_s^N(i))^2+O_N(h^2)=h\Gamma_{F_s^N}(i)+O_N(h^2)$, and two or more potential events contribute $O_N(h^2)$.

If $T=0$, the only time is $0$ and $M_0^N=0$. For $T>0$, fix $s<t$ and partition $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals of length $h=(t-s)/n$. Applying the conditional-mean estimate from step 2.1 on every subinterval, then the tower property, bounds $|\mathbb E[M_t^N-M_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]|$ by $nC_Nh^2\to0$. Thus $M^N$ is an all-pairs martingale. For fixed $N$ its paths are bounded on $[0,T]$ because the state space is finite, $H$ and its time derivative are bounded, and the compensating integrand is bounded; hence it is square-integrable.

Set $\gamma_s(\eta)=\Gamma_{F_s^N}(\eta)$ and $A_t^N=\int_0^t\gamma_s(\eta_s)ds$. If $T=0$, both processes are zero. For $T>0$, the second-moment expansion in step 2.1 and continuity of $\gamma_s(i)$ in $s$ imply $\mathbb E[A_{s+h}^N-A_s^N\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\gamma_s(\eta_s)+O_N(h^2)$: without a state change the integrand differs from $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$ by $O_N(h)$, and a state change has probability $O_N(h)$ and changes the bounded integrand over an interval of length $h$. Hence $\mathbb E[(M_{s+h}^N-M_s^N)^2-(A_{s+h}^N-A_s^N)\mid\mathcal F_s]=O_N(h^2)$. For fixed $s<t$, partition $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals and write $\Delta_jM=M_{t_{j+1}}^N-M_{t_j}^N$, $\Delta_jA=A_{t_{j+1}}^N-A_{t_j}^N$. Since $M^N$ is a martingale, $\mathbb E[M_{t_j}^N\Delta_jM\mid\mathcal F_s]=0$ by the tower property. Expanding the square, conditioning each remainder $\Delta_jM^2-\Delta_jA$ first on $\mathcal F_{t_j}$, and using the bound just proved gives an absolute conditional expectation at most $nC_Nh^2\to0$. Therefore $(M_t^N)^2-A_t^N$ is an all-pairs martingale.

The integrand $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$ is nonnegative, so $A^N$ is increasing; it is continuous and adapted. If $T=0$, the zero process is predictable. Otherwise, for each nested deterministic partition, the process equal to $A^N$ at the left endpoint on each interval $(a,b]$ and zero at time zero is predictable by [F4]; these processes converge pointwise to $A^N$ by continuity. Thus $A^N$ is predictable. At a bond $\{x,x+e_i\}$, the test-function jump is $N^{-d}(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)(H(s,x/N)-H(s,(x+e_i)/N))$. Multiplying its square by the rate $N^2$ and summing over all bonds yields the displayed formula for $\gamma_s(\eta_s)$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $|H(s,(x+e_i)/N)-H(s,x/N)|\le N^{-1}\|\partial_iH(s,\cdot)\|_\infty$; using $(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)^2\le1$ and $N^d$ bonds per coordinate gives the stated bound for $A_T^N$.

   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be a nonempty finite set, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$ with nonnegative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums, and let $\nu$ be an initial probability vector. Then there exists a uniformized realization under the conventions stated below. Its paths are càdlàg and almost surely have only finitely many event times on each bounded interval (nonexplosion), and, for all $0\le s\le t$,
$$\mathbb P(X_t=j\mid\mathcal F_s)=(e^{(t-s)L})_{X_sj}\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is the construction filtration. In particular, $e^{tL}$ is the transition matrix from any initial state.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
defines $dP_\theta=\rho_\theta\,dm$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]].
For any integrable real $A$, write $\langle A\rangle_\theta:=\int A\,dP_\theta$;
for square-integrable real $A,B$, define
$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_\theta)(B-\langle B\rangle_\theta)\,dP_\theta$.
These extend the phase-space conventions of
[[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]] to the present measure space.
Then
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim:
For every nonempty compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ and every $x\in X$, [F7] gives $|\eta\cdot T(x)-\eta'\cdot T(x)|\le\|\eta-\eta'\|_2\|T(x)\|_2$; hence $\eta\mapsto\eta\cdot T(x)$ is continuous. It attains a finite maximum $M_C(x)$ on $C$ by [F4]. Define
$$G_C(x):=w(x)\exp(M_C(x))\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{k}|T_j(x)|^2\right).$$
The exponential is finite and positive at this real input by [F5, F8], and the sum is finite, so $G_C$ is finite and nonnegative at every $x$. It is integrable under counting measure by [F2]. Since $\eta\cdot T(x)\le M_C(x)$ for every $\eta\in C$, monotonicity of $\exp$ [F9] shows that $G_C$ dominates
$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)}(1+\sum_j|T_j(x)|^2)$ for every $\theta\in C$. Thus the counting-measure model satisfies the envelope hypotheses of [F1]. Applying [F1] gives $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$, $A\in C^2(\mathbb R^k)$, and the normalized probability mass function $\pi_\theta$.

Since every summand in $Z(\theta)$ is positive and finite [F5, F8], each $\pi_\theta(x)>0$. Also $\exp(A(\theta))=Z(\theta)$ by [F6], so $e^{-A(\theta)}=1/Z(\theta)$ by [F8]. Summing the defining formula over finite $X$ therefore gives $\sum_{x\in X}\pi_\theta(x)=e^{-A(\theta)}Z(\theta)=1$. Hence the Definition gives a probability vector with full support for every finite $\theta$.

$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph: $V$ and the edge-label set $E$ are finite, and each $e\in E$ has a singleton or two-element endpoint set $\partial e\subseteq V$. Distinct labels may have the same endpoint set. Let $B\subseteq V$ be a designated boundary set and let $\xi$ be an equivalence relation on $B$; vertices in each $\xi$-class are wired together, while vertices outside $B$ remain separate. For $A\subseteq E$, let $k_\xi(A)$ be the number of connected components, including isolated vertices, after wiring the $\xi$-classes and opening exactly the edges in $A$. A loop does not join distinct vertices.

For $q\in[1,\infty)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK weight of $A$ and its partition function are

$$w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)},\qquad Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}:=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A).$$

The finite FK random-cluster probability is $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)/Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$. Every weight is positive and finite, and the finite sum $Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ is positive and finite. The free boundary condition is the identity partition on $B$; the wired boundary condition identifies all vertices of $B$ in one class.

When $G$ is a finite simple graph with the Potts/FK convention of the earlier finite Potts definition, $\xi$ is free, $q=Q$ is an integer at least two, and every activity equals $v=p/(1-p)$, this definition gives the same normalized FK law, since $w_{FK}(A)=(1-p)^{-|E|}w_{G,p,Q}^{\xi}(A)$.

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

derivations.claim: If $n<m$, condition the law on $E_m$ on edges outside $E_n$. Its induced partition on $B_n$ refines the wired partition and is coarser than the free partition. By [F2], free laws increase under restriction as volume grows and wired laws decrease. Every all-open event on a fixed finite set therefore has a bounded monotone sequence of probabilities. An atom prescribing open edges $O$ and closed edges $H$ has probability $\sum_{T\subseteq H}(-1)^{|T|}\phi(\text{all edges of }O\cup T\text{ open})$. Finite inclusion-exclusion gives the limit of every atom and hence every cylinder event. Limits of finite sums preserve positivity, normalization and all restriction-consistency identities. No measure extension is used.

Write $h=\log(p/(1-p))$ and $v=e^h$. For $Q_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^2$ define the activity sum and its volume normalization
$$Y_N^b(h)=\sum_{A\subseteq E(Q_N)}e^{h|A|}q^{k_b(A)},\qquad F_N^b(h)=N^{-2}\log Y_N^b(h).$$
The finite law is unchanged by replacing the original weights by these activity weights. Since $1\leq q^{k(A)}\leq q^{N^2}$ and $|E(Q_N)|=2N(N-1)$, one has $0\leq F_N^0(h)\leq\log q+2\log(1+e^h)$. For fixed $L$, write $N=kL+s$, $0\leq s<L$, tile the $kL$-square by $k^2$ disjoint $L$-squares, and leave the remaining vertices as singletons. Restricting the sum to configurations closing every interpiece edge gives
$$Y_N^0(h)\geq (Y_L^0(h))^{k^2}q^{N^2-k^2L^2}.$$
Closed edges have activity factor $1$ and component factors multiply over the pieces. Hence $\liminf_NF_N^0(h)\geq F_L^0(h)$ for each $L$. The finite bound above and $F_N^0\leq\sup_LF_L^0$ prove that $F(h)=\lim_NF_N^0(h)=\sup_LF_L^0(h)$ exists and is finite.

The same comparison holds for any two nested translated boxes. For a fixed $z\in\mathbb Z^2$, put $r=\|z\|_\infty$; then $\Lambda_{n-r}\subseteq\Lambda_n+z\subseteq\Lambda_{n+r}$. For every fixed increasing cylinder event, the translated free probability is sandwiched between those from the two unshifted boxes, with reverse order for wired probabilities. Their limits coincide by step 1.1. Inclusion-exclusion gives equality for all cylinders. Quarter-turn invariance holds already in each centered finite box. Thus each edge orientation and position has the same limiting open probability $u_b(p,q)$. Parameter monotonicity and $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$ follow from [F2]. For an arbitrary-boundary cylinder limit $\nu$, condition on the exterior of a fixed box $\Lambda_r$, use $\phi^0_r(C)\leq\nu_j(C)\leq\phi^1_r(C)$ for increasing $C$ supported inside it, pass to the given numerical limit, then let $r\to\infty$. This proves the asserted sandwich.

Wiring boundary vertices lowers component counts by an integer between $0$ and $|\partial Q_N|-1$, so
$$q^{-(|\partial Q_N|-1)}Y_N^0(h)\leq Y_N^\xi(h)\leq Y_N^0(h).$$
As $|\partial Q_N|\leq4N$, every boundary partition has the same pressure limit $F(h)$. Differentiating the finite sums gives
$$(F_N^b)'(h)=N^{-2}\mathbb E^b_{Q_N,h,q}|A|,\qquad (F_N^b)''(h)=N^{-2}\operatorname{Var}^b_{Q_N,h,q}(|A|)\geq0.$$
Thus these functions and their finite pointwise limit $F$ are convex.

Ordered secant slopes of a finite convex function have finite one-sided limits $F'_-(h)\leq F'_+(h)$, bounded locally by secants to fixed points on either side. If $h<k$ then $F'_+(h)\leq F'_-(k)$. Therefore the nonempty intervals $(F'_-(h),F'_+(h))$ at nondifferentiability points are pairwise disjoint. Assign each its first rational in a fixed enumeration: this is an injection into a countable set. Let $D_q$ be the image of these at most countably many $h$ under $h\mapsto e^h/(1+e^h)$. At a differentiability point, for each $t>0$ convexity gives
$$\frac{F_N^b(h)-F_N^b(h-t)}{t}\leq(F_N^b)'(h)\leq\frac{F_N^b(h+t)-F_N^b(h)}{t}.$$
Pass to lower and upper numerical limits as $N\to\infty$, then let $t\downarrow0$; the common pressure limit proves $(F_N^b)'(h)\to F'(h)$ for both boundaries.

Finite free edge probabilities in $Q_N$ are at most the infinite-volume numerical value $u_0$, and finite wired ones are at least $u_1$, by nested-box comparison and step 2.1. Thus
$$(F_N^0)'(h)\leq(2-2/N)u_0\leq(2-2/N)u_1\leq(F_N^1)'(h).$$
At $p\notin D_q$ both outside quantities tend to $F'(h)$, so $u_0=u_1$. For an arbitrary cylinder event $C$ supported on $H$, use the common-uniform ordered finite heat-bath chains from [F2]. At every time the difference of their $C$ probabilities in absolute value is at most their probability of differing on $H$, which by order and a union bound is at most the sum over $e\in H$ of their mean edge differences. Let time tend to infinity, then the finite box tend to the lattice. This gives
$$|\pi^1_{p,q}(C)-\pi^0_{p,q}(C)|\leq |H|(u_1-u_0)=0.$$
This proves equality of the numerical families, without constructing an infinite coupling or law.

If $p<p'$, select one $t\in(p,p')\setminus D_q$. Such a point exists because a countable set cannot fill a real interval; it requires no sequence of arbitrary choices. For every increasing cylinder event $C$,
$$\pi^1_{p,q}(C)\leq\pi^1_{t,q}(C)=\pi^0_{t,q}(C)\leq\pi^0_{p',q}(C).$$
Apply this to $D_r$ and take the infimum over $r$ to obtain $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$. Finally let $a_n=\phi^1_{n,p,q}(D_n)$. For $m\geq r$, truncation of a path at its first smaller-boundary hit and [F2] give $a_m\leq\phi^1_{m,p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. In particular $a_n$ decreases to a real $L$. Letting $m\to\infty$ gives $L\leq\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. Taking the infimum over $r$ proves $L=\Theta_1(p,q)$.
