The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument. Let $K:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint and positive, meaning $\langle Kx,x\rangle\ge0$ for $x\in D(K)$. Let $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ be a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iK$: its strong derivative at zero exists exactly on $D(K)$ and equals $iKx$. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the complement of the set of $z$ for which $K-z:D(K)\to\mathcal H$ has a bounded everywhere-defined inverse.

For every $x,y\in\mathcal H$ there is a finite complex Borel measure $\mu_{x,y}$ on $[0,\infty)$ such that

$$\langle U_t x,y\rangle=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{itE}\,d\mu_{x,y}(E),\qquad |\mu_{x,y}|([0,\infty))\le\|x\|\,\|y\|.$$

The measures are sesquilinear in $(x,y)$, $\mu_x:=\mu_{x,x}$ is positive with total mass $\|x\|^2$, and every $\mu_{x,y}$ is carried by $\sigma(K)$. If $P_0$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\ker K$, then

$$\mu_{x,y}(\{0\})=\langle P_0x,y\rangle.$$

In particular, if $\sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[g,\infty)$ with $g>0$, the measures $\mu_{(I-P_0)x,(I-P_0)y}$ are carried by $[g,\infty)$. Spectral measures and a projection-valued spectral resolution are not assumptions of this statement.

For $t>0$ and $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e(-x\xi)\,dx$,
$$\widehat{e^{-\pi t x^2}}(\xi)=t^{-1/2}e^{-\pi\xi^2/t}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

derivations.claim: The positive and negative frequency measures $$\mu_+=\mu_{Qb\Omega,Qa^*\Omega},\qquad \mu_-=\mu_{Qa\Omega,Qb^*\Omega}$$ are carried by $[g,\infty)$ and each has total variation at most $\|A\|\|B\|$, since $\pi$ and $Q$ are contractions. Using $U_t\Omega=\Omega$ and the linear-first pairing gives $$\omega(AB)-\omega(A)\omega(B)=\mu_+([g,\infty)),\qquad f(t)=\int e^{itE}d\mu_+(E)-\int e^{-itE}d\mu_-(E).$$ Indeed $\omega(A\alpha_t(B))=\langle U_tb\Omega,a^*\Omega\rangle$ and $\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)=\langle U_{-t}a\Omega,b^*\Omega\rangle$. Their ground-vector terms are both $\omega(A)\omega(B)$ and cancel. Commutativity also gives $f(0)=0$.

For $\varepsilon>0$, the exponential primitive and its limit at infinity in [F4] give $1/(\varepsilon+it)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon w}e^{-itw}dw$. The Gaussian factor makes the resulting double integral absolutely integrable, with majorant $e^{-qt^2}e^{-\varepsilon w}$ of finite integral. Hence [F2] and [F3] give $$h_{q,\varepsilon}(E):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-qt^2}e^{itE}}{2\pi(\varepsilon+it)}dt=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi q}}\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon w}e^{-(E-w)^2/(4q)}dw.$$ It lies between zero and one and converges as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to $h_q(E)$ given by the same right side without $e^{-\varepsilon w}$. For $E\ge g$, substituting $u=(E-w)/(2\sqrt q)$ in its complementary Gaussian tail gives $$0\le1-h_q(E)=h_q(-E)\le\tfrac12 e^{-E^2/(4q)}\le\tfrac12 e^{-g^2/(4q)}.$$ For completeness, the tail estimate is $\int_z^\infty e^{-u^2}du\le e^{-z^2}\int_0^\infty e^{-v^2}dv$ for $z\ge0$, obtained by $u=z+v$ and $(z+v)^2\ge z^2+v^2$; the Gaussian integral in [F2] normalizes the final half.

The unregularized time integrand is integrable near zero because $|f(t)|/|t|\le L$ there. Away from zero, $|f(t)|\le2\|A\|\|B\|$, so the Gaussian divided by $|t|$ is an integrable majorant on each tail. For $t\ne0$ one has $|\varepsilon+it|\ge|t|$. Dominated convergence in time thus proves $I_{q,\varepsilon}\to I_q(A,B)$, and also establishes the asserted absolute convergence without a principal-value convention.

Insert the two measures of step 1.1 into the regularized integral $I_{q,\varepsilon}=\int e^{-qt^2}f(t)/(2\pi(\varepsilon+it))dt$. Scalar Fubini is legitimate at fixed $\varepsilon>0$: their finite variations and the integrable Gaussian divided by $\varepsilon$ give an absolute majorant. Equivalently apply it to the four positive measures in each polarization formula of [F1]. Therefore $$I_{q,\varepsilon}=\int h_{q,\varepsilon}(E)d\mu_+(E)-\int h_{q,\varepsilon}(-E)d\mu_-(E).$$ The bound $0\le h_{q,\varepsilon}\le1$ and finite variations permit dominated convergence on these measures. Its limit is $\int h_q(E)d\mu_+-\int h_q(-E)d\mu_-$.

By steps 1.1, 2.1 and 1.3, the difference from the connected correlation is the sum of an integral of $1-h_q(E)$ against $\mu_+$ and an integral of $h_q(-E)$ against $\mu_-$. Both measures are carried by $E\ge g$. Step 1.2 bounds each multiplier by $\tfrac12e^{-g^2/(4q)}$, and step 1.1 bounds each variation by $\|A\|\|B\|$. The two halves give exactly the stated estimate, with no factor from replacing $A,B$ by centered operators.

Let $Q\in\{2,3,4\}$, $L\ge1$, $\omega_Q=e^{2\pi i/Q}$, and $\delta=\sqrt Q$. On $\mathbb C^Q$ with basis $|0\rangle,\ldots,|Q-1\rangle$, define the clock and shift matrices by
$$R_Q|a\rangle=\omega_Q^a|a\rangle,\qquad M_Q|a\rangle=|a-1\!\pmod Q\rangle.$$
Thus the source matrices are

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\mathcal L:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Define $T_t:=e^{t\mathcal L}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^n\mathcal L^n/n!$ for $t\geq0$, and assume that each $T_t$ is completely positive and trace-preserving; the exponential gives $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$. Let $\sigma=\sigma^*>0$ satisfy $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1$ and $T_t(\sigma)=\sigma$ for every $t\geq0$. A density matrix $\rho$ means $\rho=\rho^*$, $v^*\rho v\geq0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^d$, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. For such a density matrix $\rho$, define the finite quantum relative entropy

$$D(\rho\|\sigma):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),$$

using the natural logarithm, the finite spectral logarithm on the support of $\rho$, and $0\log0:=0$. Since $\sigma$ is positive definite, $D(\rho\|\sigma)$ is finite for every density $\rho$. Then $t\mapsto D(T_t\rho\|\sigma)$ is nonincreasing on $[0,\infty)$. If $t$ is interpreted as seconds, $\mathcal L$ has units seconds$^{-1}$; the statement is mathematical and asserts no physical applicability. At every $t\geq0$ for which $\rho_t:=T_t\rho$ is positive definite, its derivative exists (as a right derivative at $t=0$) and

$$\frac{d}{dt}D(\rho_t\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\mathcal L(\rho_t)(\log\rho_t-\log\sigma)\right)\leq0.$$

At singular $\rho_t$ this logarithmic derivative is not asserted; the extended-real upper right Dini derivative is at most zero. No detailed-balance assumption, strict decay, unique stationary state, or convergence to $\sigma$ is asserted.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

Each bond contributes at least $-J$, with equality exactly when $s_j=s_{j+1}$. Since the open chain is connected, all bonds attain equality exactly for the two constant configurations; for $N=1$ the empty bond sum leaves its two basis configurations degenerate as well.

At $J=0$, a $Z$-basis configuration $s\in\{-1,1\}^N$ has energy $-h\sum_js_j$. If $h>0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=1$; if $h<0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=-1$. Thus the unique minimizing $Z$-configuration has the orientation stated in the Example.

For $\beta>0$, [F2] gives the stated product trace for the exact $H_N$ of [F1] and its open-chain energies. The trace itself is the ordinary trace of the finite matrix exponential on the $2^N$-dimensional space.

For an endomorphism $C$ of $\mathcal H_N$, use the operator norm $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup\{\|C\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}:\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}=1\}$ from the finite product inner product. The entries of $-\beta H_N(h,J)$ are polynomials in $\beta,h,J$. On each compact set of complex parameter triples this matrix has a finite uniform operator-norm bound $C$. Define its complex-parameter exponential by $\exp(-\beta H_N)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(-\beta H_N)^m/m!$; the summands have norm at most $C^m/m!$, so the series converges uniformly on each such compact set. The matrix exponential power series is holomorphic in its entries (that is, locally represented by convergent complex power series), so composing it with the polynomial matrix entries makes each matrix entry, and its finite trace, holomorphic in $(\beta,h,J)$. Their restrictions to $\mathbb R^3$ are real-analytic in the sense defined in the Statement. For real parameters, [F3]'s spectral exponential agrees with this series by applying the scalar exponential series to each real eigenvalue $\lambda_r$ of the Hermitian $H_N$; hence $Z_N=\sum_re^{-\beta\lambda_r}>0$. This proves analyticity for each fixed finite $N$ only; it gives no conclusion about the existence or analyticity of a limit as $N\to\infty$.

is real orthogonal. The tensor-factor operators commute on $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}$; expanding their commutators and applying [F5] gives $[b,b^\dagger]=[d,d^\dagger]=I$ and $[b,d^\dagger]=[b,d]=0$ on that core. Since $\Psi_\omega\in D$, the operator $b\Psi_\omega$ is defined, and
$$b\Psi_\omega=\alpha(a_{\mathbb C}(1)\psi_\omega)\otimes\Omega_e+\beta\,\psi_\omega\otimes(e\Omega_e).$$
The environment term vanishes because $e\Omega_e=0$. Therefore $\mathfrak n_{\rm out}(\omega)=\|b\Psi_\omega\|^2=\alpha^2\|a_{\mathbb C}(1)\psi_\omega\|^2=\Gamma n_\omega$, by the quadratic-form definition in the Statement.

In [F3] take $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$ and $b=\kappa/2$. For the seconds-frequency variable, Fourier change of variables gives $S_k(\omega)=\chi S_\kappa(\omega/\chi)$, hence $S_k(\omega)=\omega/[2(e^{2\pi\omega/k}-1)]$ away from zero and $S_k(0)=\chi\kappa/(4\pi)=k/(4\pi)$. Substitution of $-\omega$ and cancellation of the common factor gives $S_k(-\omega)=e^{2\pi\omega/k}S_k(\omega)$ for $\omega>0$.

Put $x=\theta\omega>0$. By the mean-value theorem [F9] on $[0,x]$, for some $c\in(0,x)$, $\exp(x)-\exp(0)=x\exp'(c)=x\exp(c)>0$, using [F8] and [F7]; [F6] gives $\exp(0)=1$. Hence $n_\theta(\omega)>0$ and $0<\Gamma_*(\omega)<1$. If any filter has $\Gamma(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_\theta(\omega)$ at every positive frequency, division by this positive value gives $\Gamma(\omega)=1$ everywhere, so no nonconstant filter preserves the same width. If $0<\omega_1<\omega_2$, applying [F9] on $[\theta\omega_1,\theta\omega_2]$ gives $\exp(\theta\omega_2)-\exp(\theta\omega_1)=\theta(\omega_2-\omega_1)\exp'(c)>0$ for some intermediate $c$, by [F8] and [F7]. Thus $\Gamma_*$ is nonconstant. By [F10], $\exp(2x)-1=(\exp(x)-1)(\exp(x)+1)$; therefore $\Gamma_*(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=1/(\exp(2x)-1)=n_{2\theta}(\omega)$. The varying filter can thus produce a Planck occupation at a different width.

citations.quote: For a finite fusion transfer count model, let $e_0\in\mathbb R^I$ be the coordinate vector equal to $1$ at label $0$ and $0$ elsewhere, and define $v_n:=N^n e_0$. Then $v_0=e_0$, $v_{n+1}=Nv_n$, and the number of length-$n$ paths from $0$ to a label $a$ is $(v_n)_a=(N^n)_{a0}$. Whenever $D_n>0$, the operator $\rho_n=D_n^{-1}I_{\mathbb C^{D_n}}$ is a density matrix and has von Neumann entropy $s(\rho_n)=\log D_n$ in nats. For the supplied two-label matrix $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, with labels ordered $0,1$, one has $D_0=1$, $D_1=0$, $D_2=1$, and $D_{n+2}=D_{n+1}+D_n$ for every $n\geq0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Applying the recurrence in [F1] gives $D_2=1$, $D_3=1$, and $D_4=2$. Since $D_4>0$, the corresponding finite-state entropy is $s_4=\log2$.
With the assignment $a$, the ratio is $c(a):=s_4/A_4=\log2/(4a)$. Replacing $a$ by $2a$ leaves $N$, $D_4$, and $s_4$ fixed while giving $c(2a)=\log2/(8a)=c(a)/2$.
Because $2>1$, [F2] gives $\log2>\log1=0$; since $a>0$, $c(a)>0$ and therefore $c(2a)\neq c(a)$. The count model consequently does not fix this coefficient.
